terms.definition: A jokey “counter” to 6-7. Where 6-7 can stand in for almost anything, 41 is used as the contradictory alternative — another nonsense number kids yell back.
terms.notes: Documented in Axis’s 2026 parent slang guide as the popular contradiction to 6-7, boosted by a rap song by Blizzi Boi that repeats “41.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A mostly meaningless Gen Alpha catchphrase (said “six-seven,” not “sixty-seven”). Kids shout it as an inside joke, a “so-so” shrug, or whenever the numbers 6 or 7 appear. The point is being in on the joke, not a secret code.
terms.example: Teacher writes 67 on the board and the whole class yells “six-seven!”
terms.notes: Dictionary.com’s 2025 Word of the Year. Tied to Skrilla’s song “Doot Doot (6 7),” TikToks, and NBA player LaMelo Ball (6'7"). Also written 67, 6 7, or six-seven.

terms.definition: Coded words people use online so algorithms don’t hide the post (unalive, seggs, grape).
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: self-censored language used to bypass content moderation.

terms.definition: Did something so well there’s nothing left to improve. Often “ate and left no crumbs.” Not about food.
terms.example: “She sang the whole song a cappella. Ate and left no crumbs.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026 and WeAreLuna 2026. Related to “devoured” / “served.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: The vibe or cool-factor someone gives off. Not mystical — more like “main-character energy.” Doing something impressive “gives aura.”
terms.example: “He hit the game-winner. His aura goes crazy.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026: “describes the vibe somebody gives off.” Related to the scoring joke “aura points.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Deliberately doing small, cool-looking things to look effortlessly impressive — posing, walking slowly off the court, posting gym pics for the vibe.
terms.example: “Posting a silent gym selfie every morning is just aura farming.”
terms.notes: On Dictionary.com’s 2025 Word of the Year shortlist and Oxford’s 2025 shortlist (“deliberate cultivation of an impressive public persona”).

trendingEvidence.headline: Official Word of the Year — stays trending per policy

terms.definition: A pretend scoreboard for how cool you are. You “gain aura points” for something smooth and “lose aura points” for something awkward.
terms.example: “He lost aura points for tripping on the way to the free-throw line.”
terms.notes: Documented by Axis (2026) and Bark (2026). In August 2026 news, cities even used “aura points” in teen e-bike safety campaigns.

terms.definition: A compliment: a confident, stylish, attractive woman. “Bad” here means good.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; also Axis / Wikipedia 2020s glossary.

terms.definition: Unbothered by what other people think; speaking your mind. Can also mean “I agree with that take.”
terms.example: “He wore the same hoodie all week. Based.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “unconcerned with what others think.”

terms.definition: Unoriginal — into only the most mainstream things. Often teasing, not a deep insult.
terms.example: “Pumpkin spice in September? A little basic.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026: someone who lacks originality and likes predictable mainstream things.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Staying in bed for hours on purpose — scrolling, snacking, not being productive. Can be a cozy protest or a mental-health red flag, depending on how often it happens.
terms.example: “Saturday is for bed rot. Do not disturb.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026: lying in bed for hours, sometimes as a critique of hustle culture.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A quirk that isn’t good or bad — just oddly specific. Between a red flag (warning) and a green flag (good sign).
terms.example: “His beige flag is that he sleeps in his shirts backwards.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026. Dating-app language that kids now use about anyone’s habits.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Best friend. Used sincerely or sarcastically (“okay bestie”).
terms.notes: Axis 2026. Everyday teen English, online and off.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A casual “okay,” “deal,” or “you bet.” Agreement, not a wager.
terms.notes: Axis 2026 and Yahoo 2026: a shortened “you bet” used as an interjected yes.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Fancy, extra, or trying to look high-class. From “bourgeois.” Can be a compliment or a tease.
terms.notes: Axis 2026. Also spelled boujee.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: The foggy, fried feeling after too much mindless scrolling — or the junk content itself. Teens say it jokingly about their own TikTok habits.
terms.example: “I watched skibidi compilations for an hour. Peak brain rot.”
terms.notes: Oxford’s 2024 Word of the Year; still listed as current in Axis and Bark’s 2026 parent guides. Also written brainrot.

terms.definition: Bros / guy friends. Part of the -uzz family (huzz, bruzz, gruzz).
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; WeAreLuna’s huzz explainer lists bruzz as male friends.

terms.definition: Really, really good — almost always about food. Doubled for extra praise: “bussin’ bussin’.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026. AAVE that went mainstream via TikTok food reviews.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A formative moment you just have to live through — awkward, hard, or lucky — as if it were written into your story.
terms.example: “Failing the driving test is a canon event.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a formative life experience; a relatable episode of good fortune or hardship.”

terms.definition: A lie or exaggeration. Opposite of “no cap.”
terms.example: “He said he met her. That’s cap.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026: Cap / No Cap = lying, or not lying.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Caught doing something wrong or embarrassing, with clear proof (as if filmed in 4K).
terms.example: “Mom saw the grades portal. Caught in 4K.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: Talking to an imaginary audience the way a livestreamer says “chat.” Kids say it out loud to nobody in particular.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang (streamer talk that left the internet).

terms.definition: Trying too hard / outdated millennial-cool. Off-trend in a try-hard way.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: A silly fill-in phrase with no set meaning — like 6-7. From a song that just repeats “chicken, banana.” Kids use it as a joke answer to anything.
terms.notes: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026 and Clarion Ledger (2026): a nonsense stand-in that never unseated 6-7.
terms.sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

terms.definition: Unattractive or undesirable — of a person or a thing. “He’s chopped” = not cute.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang, citing The New York Times (Aug 2025): “unattractive, ugly, not good looking.” Roots in African American English.

terms.definition: a less attractive version of someone or something
terms.notes: Copied from Merriam-Webster’s live slang dictionary on 2026-08-12 after it appeared in today's slang news.

terms.definition: So deep in the internet that real life is the side quest. Often a tease.
terms.notes: Common 2020s descriptor in parent and culture writing about teen internet use.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of 2020s slang (related internet slang)

terms.definition: A mocking nickname for a clumsy or annoying AI / robot — the way someone might mutter at a chatbot that just made something up.
terms.example: “The homework helper just invented a citation. Stupid clanker.”
terms.notes: Macquarie Dictionary’s 2025 honourable mentions: colloquial, often derogatory, for an AI system doing human tasks poorly.

terms.definition: Notice it / mark it / I see what you did. A “gotcha” or “write that down.”
terms.notes: A middle-school teacher and students listed “clock it” among top-tier terms in a 2025 Scripps/NBC classroom interview, alongside 6-7 and huzz.
terms.sourceName: NBC 26 / Scripps News classroom slang report (2025)

terms.definition: Attention, fame, or online popularity. “Clout chasing” = doing things just to get noticed.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: In big trouble, exhausted, or done for. “I’m so cooked” = this will not end well. Different from “cooking,” which means doing well.
terms.example: “If Mom sees this grade I’m cooked.”
terms.notes: Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ slang guide. Contrast with “let him cook.”
terms.sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

terms.definition: To snap — do something reckless or overly emotional because you’re not okay. Can mean a real spiral or just “I’m about to lose it.”
terms.example: “My crush left me on read. I’m about to crash out.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026: “to do something dangerous or reckless that you might regret because you aren’t feeling emotionally stable.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Secondhand-embarrassment level awkward. If something is cringey, people want to look away.
terms.example: “Dad dancing at the barbecue is cringey.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026: “cringe-worthy, awkward.” Also just “cringe.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Cold-weather stretch when people pair up so they are not single all winter.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: Delusional — usually said jokingly about an unrealistic crush or plan. Audaciously self-confident.
terms.example: “She thinks that celebrity liked her comment. She’s delulu.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “delusional; audaciously self-confident.”

terms.definition: Great style — clothes, sneakers, accessories. “He has drip” means he looks put-together and fashionable.
terms.notes: Bark 2026: “style, great fashion sense, flashy accessories.” Hip-hop fashion slang that kids still use.

terms.definition: Agreement — “true,” “I agree.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Close friends, treated like family. A greeting as much as a noun.
terms.notes: Bark 2026. Older hip-hop / internet slang that kids still use for their friend group.

terms.definition: Playfully stealing a bite of someone else’s food. Named after streamer Fanum.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “taking someone else’s food; an Internet gibberish term.”

terms.definition: Going to / about to. From “fixing to.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026: a contraction of “fixing to.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A second, more private Instagram — “fake Insta.” Often for close friends only. Can also be used to lurk on someone quietly.
terms.example: “I posted that on my finsta, not the real one.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026; Bark 2026. Merriam-Webster has also entered the word.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Amazing or excellent. Also the 🔥 emoji.
terms.notes: Bark 2026 and Axis 2026 parent guides.

terms.definition: Showing off an outfit (or several) — usually a quick video or photo dump. “Fit” = outfit.
terms.notes: WeAreLuna 2026: showing off your outfit, often as a social-video trend.

terms.definition: To show off. Can be a verb (“stop flexing”) or a noun (“that’s a flex”). Not always an insult — sometimes just bragging rights.
terms.example: “Not to flex, but we have early dismissal.”
terms.notes: WeAreLuna and Gabb 2026 parent guides. Older gym slang (“flex your muscles”) applied to anything brag-worthy.

terms.definition: A stretch when nothing is working — looks, posts, or life. Temporary, usually joked about.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; WeAreLuna 2026 also lists it.

terms.definition: Fear of missing out.
terms.notes: Bark 2026.

terms.definition: “For real.” Agreement or emphasis. “BFFR” / “be so FR” = “be serious.”
terms.notes: WeAreLuna 2026. Axis also lists BFFR / BFR / Be So FR as expressions of disbelief.

terms.definition: A blank, deadpan look younger workers or teens give when a request feels obvious, awkward, or “boomer.” Not always rude on purpose — sometimes it’s just the face.
terms.example: “I asked if they could work Saturday and got the Gen Z stare.”
terms.notes: On Dictionary.com’s 2025 Word of the Year shortlist. A workplace/culture meme about generational deadpan.

terms.definition: Suddenly ignoring someone — no texts, no explanation.
terms.notes: Common in 2026 parent slang lists (Bark, Game Quitters, Shorelight).

terms.definition: A snacky, uncooked “meal” of whatever is in the fridge — cheese, crackers, leftover fries — instead of a plated dinner.
terms.example: “Girl dinner is pickles and a string cheese.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a light meal of snacks or easy-to-prepare foods.”

terms.definition: A joking way to justify spending — “I returned something, so this purchase is free.” An inside joke; sometimes used to mock women and money.
terms.example: “I returned the shoes, so this concert is girl math free.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026 parent guide; We Are Teachers 2026 slang list.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: To over-praise someone in a way that feels fake or excessive. If a friend is “glazing” a celebrity, they’re laying it on too thick.
terms.example: “Stop glazing him — he missed half his shots.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster and Cambridge’s 2025 watchlists; Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ guide. Also “glazing.”
terms.sourceName: Merriam-Webster; Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

terms.definition: A big improvement in looks, style, or life. “She had a glow-up over the summer.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: Greatest of all time. A huge compliment.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster added GOAT / goated; still everyday teen praise.

terms.definition: A good sign in a person — the opposite of a red flag.
terms.example: “He thanked the bus driver. Green flag.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; dating-app language kids now use about anyone.

terms.definition: The opposite of low-key: obviously, seriously, not hiding it.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “straight up, seriously, extremely.”

terms.definition: Hits in a uniquely stronger or more emotional way than usual.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: Hit me up — text me / get in touch.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: Take the loss. Admit you were wrong or you lost.
terms.example: “You missed the shot. Hold the L.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “to admit being wrong or to accept defeat.” L = loss.

terms.definition: Internet slang for girls / women. Some kids use it like “crush.” It comes from a mangled, disrespectful word for women (hoes), so it is not polite even when they mean it playfully.
terms.example: “I tripped in front of the huzz.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “online slang for ‘women.’” WeAreLuna and NBC classroom reports cover the teen use.

terms.definition: Excitement around something — or the act of pumping someone up. “I finally get the hype” = I see why people like this.
terms.example: “I finally get the hype around that show.”
terms.notes: WeAreLuna 2026. Everyday sports/marketing English that teens use as a noun and verb.

terms.definition: A sudden feeling of disgust or repulsion, often about a crush’s small habit.
terms.example: “He chews with his mouth open. Instant ick.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a feeling of disgust or repulsion.”

terms.definition: I just burst out laughing. A newer stand-in for LOL.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: Used to name a vibe or look: “It’s giving 2000s movie star.”
terms.example: “That jacket? It’s giving coach on the sideline.”
terms.notes: Ballroom / internet slang listed across 2026 parent and social-media slang guides.

terms.definition: “If you know, you know.” An inside joke — if you get it, you’re in the group.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: A loss. “Take the L” = accept you lost.
terms.notes: Axis 2026.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Let someone keep going — they’re on a roll. “Cooking” = performing well. Don’t interrupt; they’re about to do something good.
terms.example: “Don’t cut him off, let him cook.”
terms.notes: Yahoo 2026 parent guide; common sports and streamer slang. Opposite vibe of “cooked.”
terms.sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

terms.definition: To enter a state of deep focus. “I’m locked in” = I’m concentrating, don’t interrupt.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “to enter a state of deep focus.”

terms.definition: Going all-in on looking more attractive — skincare, gym, sometimes extreme or unsafe advice from online forums.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: efforts, sometimes extreme, young men take to look more attractive.

terms.definition: A little / secretly / not making a big deal of it. Opposite of high-key.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster / everyday teen English; Axis and parent guides list it as current.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A mashed-up intensifier: “low-key” + “genuinely.” Used like “literally” or “honestly.” Brain-rot word-building, not a secret meaning.
terms.example: “The store is lowkenuinely out of iced tea.”
terms.notes: Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ guide, citing The New York Times: a brain-rot blend used in place of “literally,” “low-key,” or “genuinely.”

terms.definition: Acting like the star of the movie — confident, a little dramatic, center of the story.
terms.example: “Walking into school with coffee and headphones. Main character energy.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “dramatic self-confidence; obtrusive self-importance.”

terms.definition: Korean 말랑 / 말랑말랑 (mallang, mallangmallang) means soft, squishy, or fluffy. That is where the character name Molang comes from. It is a real Korean word for texture, not a teen code language.
terms.example: A Korean speaker might call a mochi “mallangmallang” — soft and squishy.
terms.notes: Hye-Ji Yoon has said Molang’s name comes from “mallang~ mallang.” Some fan wikis also note 몰라 (molla, “I don’t know”) as a look-alike, but the designer’s stated source is mallang = soft.
terms.sourceName: Korean mallang / mallangmallang; Molang name origin (Hye-Ji Yoon)

terms.definition: A tongue-posture trend claimed (without solid medical proof) to sharpen the jawline. Kids may sit in class pressing their tongue to the roof of the mouth.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a tongue technique purported to enhance one’s jaw and face.”

terms.definition: Of mediocre or disappointing quality. Not terrible — just nothing special.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: Visibly outshining someone — looking better, playing better, taking the spotlight. “He’s mogging me in this photo” = he looks way better.
terms.example: “Don’t stand next to him in group pics, he’ll mog you.”
terms.notes: From AMOG, “alpha male of the group” (noted by Psychology Today). Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ guide covers the current teen use.
terms.sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

terms.definition: The round white bunny from the kids’ show Molang. Not a secret code. The name comes from Korean 말랑말랑 (mallangmallang) — “soft, squishy, fluffy.” Kids say it like a character name, or for something cute and squishy.
terms.notes: Created by Korean illustrator Hye-Ji Yoon (2010), animated by France’s Millimages. Designer said the name is from mallang / mallangmallang. The characters do not speak English — they use a made-up sound language called Molanguese.

terms.definition: The show’s made-up “language”: cute babbles and sound effects, not real words. Millimages created it so kids anywhere can follow the feelings without translation. If your child is “speaking Molang,” they are mimicking those noises — there is no hidden vocabulary to decode.
terms.example: Molang and Piu Piu only “talk” in Molanguese on the show.
terms.notes: Millimages (official): Molanguese was created so anyone, anywhere, could understand Molang emotionally without needing words. Also called Molangish in some fan write-ups. The series is produced as non-dialogue.

terms.definition: “No lie” / “I’m serious.” “Cap” means a lie or exaggeration; “no cap” means this is the truth.
terms.example: “I didn’t study and still got an A, no cap.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026: “Cap/No Cap = Lying, or not lying.” Long-running hip-hop slang that teens still use daily.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Someone acting robotic or on autopilot, like a video-game extra with no free will. Often a tease, sometimes unkind.
terms.example: “He just repeats whatever the group says. NPC behavior.”
terms.notes: From “non-player character” in games. Common in 2020s youth slang glossaries.

terms.definition: Weird, awkward, cringeworthy, or just bad — not the state. “That’s so Ohio” = that’s bizarre. From “only in Ohio” memes that treated Ohio as a place where surreal things happen.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “weird, awkward, cringeworthy.” Also covered in parent explainers (Screenwise, Tinybeans).

terms.definition: A brush-off for an older person (or anyone sounding old) who doesn’t get it.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; Axis 2026 still lists it.

terms.definition: Acting wild, inappropriate, or way out of line.
terms.example: “Yelling at the ref like that was out of pocket.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: A one-sided “relationship” a fan feels with a celebrity, influencer, or even an AI chatbot. The famous person does not know the fan; the fan still feels close.
terms.example: “She has a parasocial thing with that podcast host — she talks like they’re friends.”
terms.notes: Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year 2025. An older psychology term that went mainstream as influencer culture and AI companions grew.
terms.sourceName: Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year 2025

trendingEvidence.headline: Official Word of the Year — stays trending per policy

terms.definition: The person who rides shotgun and does not drive — usually treated like royalty.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: End of discussion. A louder “period.”
terms.notes: Common in 2026 Gen Alpha slang lists (Hoomale and others).

terms.definition: Two different things: (1) Molang’s chick friend is named Piu Piu — kids say it like “pew pew.” (2) As slang/algospeak, “pew pew” is the laser/gun sound; Wiktionary also lists it as a firearm. Ask which one they mean.
terms.example: “He went pew pew in the game.” / (online) “No pew pews in the backpack.”
terms.notes: Wiktionary lists pew pew as a noun meaning a firearm. Parents and teachers also flag it as a censorship workaround for “gun.”

terms.definition: Someone who puts other people down to look more likable — “I’m not like other girls/guys.”
terms.example: “She called all the other girls basic. Pick-me behavior.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: Molang’s best friend: a small yellow chick. Shy, careful, the voice of reason. Kids often say the name like “pew pew.” Not a gun joke in this context — it’s the character.
terms.example: “I want the Piu Piu plush, not just Molang.”
terms.notes: Official Molang franchise (Millimages / shop.molang.com): Molang and best friend chick Piu Piu.

terms.definition: A cutesy pet name for someone you love — a partner, a best friend, even a parent.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a term of endearment.” In print since the mid-1960s; kids still use it.

terms.definition: Online content made to make you angry so you comment, share, and keep the algorithm fed. If a post seems designed to wind people up, it is probably rage bait.
terms.example: “Don’t reply — that headline is pure rage bait.”
terms.notes: Oxford University Press Word of the Year 2025, after recorded usage roughly tripled. Cousin of “clickbait,” but the hook is outrage, not curiosity.
terms.sourceName: Oxford University Press Word of the Year 2025

trendingEvidence.headline: The Oxford Word of the Year 2025 is rage bait - Oxford University Press
trendingEvidence.feed: Google News — teen & Gen Alpha slang

terms.definition: When a reply gets more likes than the original post — usually meaning the original take flopped.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang / common social-media English.

terms.definition: A warning sign — something that makes you think twice about a person or situation.
terms.example: “He got mad that I had other friends. Red flag.”
terms.notes: Long-running dating slang; still listed in current parent slang guides.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Stuck in your head. If something “lives rent-free” in your mind, you can’t stop thinking about it.
terms.example: “That song is living rent-free in my head.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: preoccupied with someone or something.

terms.definition: Short for charisma: someone’s ability to charm or flirt. “W rizz” = good game; “L rizz” or “negative rizz” = striking out.
terms.example: “He actually got her number? W rizz.”
terms.notes: From “charisma.” Oxford’s 2023 Word of the Year; still in everyday teen use and defined on Wiktionary as the ability to attract a love interest.

terms.definition: A drawn-out “wow” — surprise, impress, or “that’s a lot.” Often with a hand gesture.
terms.notes: Listed in 2026 Gen Alpha parent slang roundups as an expression of surprise or disbelief.

terms.definition: A skeptical or judging glance — or talking about that glance. “Side eye” in a text means “I’m judging this.”
terms.example: “She said she ‘forgot’ her homework… side eye.”
terms.notes: WeAreLuna 2026 and Slang.net’s daily slang (August 2026: “a disapproving glance”).

terms.definition: A detour from the main plan — like a video-game extra mission. “Stopping for snacks is a side quest.”
terms.example: “Homework is the main quest. This show is a side quest.”

terms.definition: Shorthand for a lone-wolf, self-assured type — “main character” independence. Often used half-jokingly (“sigma rizz”).
terms.example: “He skipped the party to finish his project. Sigma behavior.”

terms.definition: Someone who fawns too hard — usually over a crush — and looks a little desperate doing it.

terms.notes: Merriam-Webster: to show excessive devotion to someone.

terms.definition: A romantic thing that isn’t officially a relationship — more than friends, less than dating.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; also Shorelight’s 2026 American slang list.

terms.notes: Gabb’s 2026 parent slang list. Related to “bussin’” (usually food) and “fires.”

terms.definition: To do something extremely well. A compliment for a look, a performance, or a comeback.

terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “to underestimate, overlook, or ignore.”

terms.definition: Tiny and cute. Internet spelling of small.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; WeAreLuna 2026.

terms.definition: Looking extremely good — outfit, makeup, or waistline. A strong compliment.
terms.notes: WeAreLuna 2026. From drag / beauty slang; teens use it for clothes and looks.

terms.definition: How much people-energy someone has left. When the battery is dead, they want to go home — not because they dislike you.
terms.example: “My social battery is at 2%. I’m heading out.”
terms.notes: WeAreLuna 2026. Introvert-internet language that teens now say out loud.

terms.definition: A superfan — or the act of being one. “I stan her” = I’m a devoted fan. Can be affectionate or a little obsessive.
terms.example: “I stan that author. I’ve read everything.”
terms.notes: From Eminem’s song “Stan.” Axis 2026 still lists it as current teen vocabulary.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Backing up what you said — no empty talk. Holding a boundary or following through.
terms.example: “She said she wouldn’t go if he was there, and she didn’t. Standing on business.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026: “to double-down on something or stay strong in your conviction.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Short for suspicious or shady. Something (or someone) doesn’t add up.
terms.notes: Older slang that exploded with Among Us (2018–20). Still in Axis’s 2026 dictionary.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: To be honest.
terms.notes: Axis 2026.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Gossip. “Spill the tea” = tell me the story.
terms.notes: Axis 2026.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A blunt way to say “log off and go outside.” Used when someone is too online, too deep in an argument, or losing perspective.
terms.example: “You’ve been in the comments for three hours. Touch grass.”
terms.notes: Among Merriam-Webster’s most-looked-up words of 2025. An internet scold that became everyday slang.

terms.definition: Cool or awesome. A respelling of “tough,” not an insult.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “cool, awesome, etc.”

terms.definition: A coded way to say kill or die — used so social apps don’t flag the post. If a child uses this about themselves, treat it as a real safety signal, not a joke.
terms.example: “The movie unalived the villain in the first scene.”
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a euphemism for ‘kill’ or ‘die.’” Algospeak.

terms.definition: Short for “uncle.” A teasing name for an older person (or anyone acting old / out of touch). If your kid calls you unc, they’re saying you’re not with it.
terms.notes: Bark’s 2026 teen-slang guide: an older, usually male figure, or anyone out of touch with current trends.

terms.definition: Nailed it — did exactly what the moment called for, and then some.
terms.example: “Look at that costume. She understood the assignment.”
terms.notes: Axis 2026; We Are Teachers 2026.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Fair / I get it / that checks out.
terms.notes: Everyday Gen Z English listed across 2026 slang roundups.

terms.definition: A quick, informal read of someone’s mood or a room’s energy.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a casual or intuitive assessment of the quality of something or someone.”

terms.definition: A win. “That’s a W.” Opposite of L (a loss).
terms.notes: Axis 2026: antonym of take the L; pronounced “dub.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: October–December as a “lock-in” for goals — gym, grades, habits — before the new year. Also called the Great Lock In.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: a three-month period dedicated to focusing on goals before the new year.

terms.definition: A trombone-style “too bad” sound, used to mock a small failure.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: used to mock someone else’s misfortune or disappointment.

terms.definition: “What you look like?” A request for a photo. Bark flags this: strangers on apps often lead with WYLL — kids should be careful before sending pictures.
terms.example: “I matched with someone and the first message was WYLL.”
terms.notes: Bark 2026 teen text-codes guide.

terms.definition: Someone who talks a lot. “Yapping” = chatting nonstop. Usually affectionate, sometimes “please stop.”
terms.example: “Sorry, I’m such a yapper when I’m nervous.”
terms.notes: WeAreLuna 2026 lists yapper / yap / yapping. Related joke: “yappuccino.”

terms.definition: To pile beauty filters on a photo until it looks ultra-glam and a little fake.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “to heavily edit an image with beauty filters.” WeAreLuna 2026 also lists it.

terms.definition: You only live once — used to justify a risky or fun choice.
terms.notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

terms.definition: A hype phrase: you are the guy. The main character. The one everyone wants to be in this moment. Works for any gender in practice.
terms.example: “You cooked dinner and fixed the Wi-Fi? You’re him.”
terms.notes: Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ guide: hyping someone as the person everyone wants to be.
terms.sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

terms.definition: Laughing out loud. Often just means “that’s mildly amusing” or softens a message — actual laughter not required.
Be right back. Stepping away from the conversation briefly.
Shaking my head. Disappointment or disbelief.
Not gonna lie. Like TBH — a preface for honesty, sometimes a confession.
What (are) you doing? A conversation opener.
Got to go. Ending the conversation.
I don’t know.
Let me know.
In case you missed it. Usually introduces a repost or old news.
I swear to God. Emphasis, exasperation, or a (usually empty) threat.
In my opinion. IMHO adds “humble.”
Good game. Sportsmanship at the end of a match; “GG EZ” is the trash-talk version.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Away from keyboard. Not at the controls right now.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: A beginner or unskilled player (from “newbie”). Usually teasing, sometimes toxic.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: When developers weaken something in an update. Named after the foam toy brand.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: The opposite of nerf — making a character or item stronger.
terms.example: “Healers got a huge buff this patch.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Doing repetitive tasks to level up or earn in-game rewards. Not misbehavior — it’s farming XP.
terms.example: “I spent all weekend grinding for that skin.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Items, gear, or currency collected in-game. “Loot boxes” are randomized (and controversial) versions.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: An experienced player using a new low-rank account to stomp beginners. Widely considered unsporting.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Winning under extreme pressure, often as the last player standing. “He clutched it.”
terms.example: “1v4 and he still clutched the round.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Coming back to life after dying in-game, usually after a short wait.
terms.example: “I respawn in 10 seconds, hold the point.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Network delay that makes the game stutter or freeze. The universal excuse for losing.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Enemy attention. “Pulling aggro” means making enemies target you — a tank’s whole job.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: The durable teammate whose role is soaking damage so fragile teammates survive.
terms.example: “We need a tank before we can queue.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Player versus player — competing against real people instead of computer enemies (PvE).
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Quitting a game mid-match out of frustration, often dramatically.
terms.example: “He rage quit after the third loss.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Excitement or hype, from the Twitch “PogChamp” emote. Also “pog” or “poggers moment.”
“Looks good to me” — the standard code-review approval. Sometimes suspiciously fast.
Explaining your code line-by-line to an inanimate object (classically a rubber duck) until you spot the bug yourself.
A chain of small side-tasks you must finish before the task you actually wanted to do — each one seemingly necessary.
terms.example: “I came to fix a typo and ended up upgrading the build system. Total yak shave.”

terms.definition: Spending disproportionate time debating trivial details (the bike shed’s color) while ignoring the hard, important stuff.
terms.example: “Two hours on the button color — pure bikeshedding.”

terms.definition: The future cost of choosing a quick fix now instead of the proper solution. It accrues interest.
terms.example: “We shipped fast, but the tech debt is piling up.”

terms.definition: Tangled, hard-to-follow code with no clear structure — everything connects to everything.
terms.example: “Nobody touches that module. It’s pure spaghetti.”

terms.definition: Meaningless placeholder names used in examples when the actual name doesn’t matter.
terms.example: “Just call the function foo for the demo.”

terms.definition: “You aren’t gonna need it” — don’t build features on speculation; wait until they’re actually required.
terms.example: “Skip the plugin system for now. YAGNI.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — You aren’t gonna need it

terms.definition: “Don’t repeat yourself” — every piece of logic should live in exactly one place.
terms.example: “Extract that into a helper. Keep it DRY.”

terms.definition: How many people can leave (or be hit by a bus) before a project is doomed because only they understood it. A bus factor of 1 is scary.
terms.example: “Only Dana knows the deploy script — bus factor of one.”

terms.definition: A company using its own product internally — “eating your own dog food” — to find problems before customers do.
terms.example: “We’ve been dogfooding the new app all month.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Eating your own dog food

terms.definition: A bug that disappears or changes behavior the moment you try to observe or debug it. Named after the uncertainty principle.
terms.example: “It crashes in production but never in the debugger. Classic heisenbug.”

terms.definition: A surface symptom in code that hints at a deeper design problem — not a bug, but a warning sign.
Release it to users — often said with a mix of confidence and reckless optimism.
To return to a topic later. Sometimes sincere; sometimes where topics go to die.
terms.example: “Let’s circle back on that after the quarter.”

terms.definition: The claim that combining two things creates extra value. The classic buzzword, beloved in mergers.
Capacity to take on work. “No bandwidth” = a polite no.
terms.example: “I don’t have the bandwidth for another project.”

terms.definition: The easiest wins available — quick tasks with visible payoff.
terms.example: “Fix the signup bug first, that’s low-hanging fruit.”

terms.definition: To move a discussion out of the current meeting — usually because it’s off-topic or getting awkward.
A meeting end-time that genuinely cannot slip. A pre-announced escape hatch.
A thorough examination of a topic, as opposed to a high-level overview.
terms.example: “Next week we’ll do a deep dive on churn.”

terms.definition: To attempt something impossibly broad instead of scoping it down. Usually a warning: don’t.
terms.example: “Let’s not boil the ocean — pick one market first.”

terms.definition: To make a measurable difference on a metric that matters.
terms.example: “Will this feature actually move the needle?”

terms.definition: Send me a quick message. Borrowed from network terminology.
To float an idea to leadership and see how they react (“…and see who salutes”).
terms.example: “I’ll run it up the flagpole before we commit.”

terms.definition: To attempt to reconcile two things that seem fundamentally incompatible — from the famously impossible geometry problem.
terms.example: “Cutting costs while doubling quality? We’re squaring the circle.”

terms.definition: Oh my God/gosh. Surprise, excitement, or horror — the all-purpose exclamation.
terms.example: “omg did you see who just walked in”

terms.definition: Laughing my a** off. One notch stronger than LOL.
By the way. Introduces a side note.
For your information. Sharing something you should know — sometimes passive-aggressively.
Never mind. Retracting or dropping the previous message.
terms.example: “where are my keys? nvm found them.”

terms.definition: Just kidding. Marks the previous message as a joke.
Right now.
In real life — offline, as opposed to on the internet.
terms.example: “We finally met irl after two years of gaming together.”

terms.definition: Point of view. On social media it captions a video showing a scene “from your perspective” — often used loosely for any relatable scenario.
terms.example: “POV: you’re the last one picked in gym class.”

terms.definition: Talk to you later.
On my way. Sometimes sent before actually leaving.
Where you at? Asking someone’s location.
What about you? Bouncing the question back.
How about you? Interchangeable with WBU.
I love you. Between friends as much as romance.
I don’t care. Can be genuine indifference or a brush-off.
Too much information. You’ve overshared.
terms.example: “I did NOT need to hear that. tmi.”

terms.definition: For what it’s worth. Softens an opinion or minor contribution.
terms.example: “fwiw I thought your speech was great.”

terms.definition: If I recall correctly. Hedges a statement from memory.
As far as I know. Another hedge — true to my knowledge.
To be fair. Adds nuance or gives credit before/after criticism.
Of course.
No problem. Response to thanks.
That feeling when. Captions a relatable emotional moment, often with an image.
terms.example: “tfw the vending machine eats your dollar.”

terms.definition: On God. Swearing something is true — a stronger “fr.”
Piss(es) me off. Venting annoyance. (In some circles also “put me on” = recommend me something — context matters.)
One true pairing — the fictional (or real) couple you root for above all others. Fandom language. Older texters may also mean “on the phone.”
terms.example: “Those two characters are my otp, don’t argue.”

terms.definition: Ambushing an opponent with surprise or superior numbers — often roaming from another lane to jump someone.
Keeping an enemy at a distance — hitting while retreating so it chases you like a kite on a string but never lands a hit.
terms.example: “Kite the boss around the pillar while we heal.”

terms.definition: Winning through a cheap, unintended, or low-effort tactic instead of “fair” skill.
terms.example: “He cheesed the boss by standing where its attacks can’t reach.”

terms.definition: Deliberately misspelled “get good” — the community’s tough-love (or mocking) response to complaints about difficulty.
The modern “git gud”: implying the problem isn’t the game, it’s you.
terms.example: “I keep falling off the map.” “Sounds like a skill issue.”

terms.definition: Utterly defeated (from a typo of “owned”). Dated but still understood everywhere.
A kill in a shooter. “Top fragger” = the player with the most kills.
Staying in one hidden spot and ambushing everyone who walks by. Effective; universally resented.
A cheat that lets a player see through walls. Suspiciously good tracking gets accused of it constantly.
terms.example: “How did he know I was there?? Wallhacks.”

terms.definition: A cheat that aims automatically. Also a (semi-)compliment for inhumanly accurate players.
Beating a game as fast as possible, often with glitches and deep route knowledge. Also used jokingly for rushing anything.
Someone playing at maximum sweatiness in a casual setting. Mild insult with a hint of respect.
terms.example: “It’s a party mode, why are you tryharding?”

terms.definition: Extremely intense, competitive play (or player) — as in literally sweating over a casual match.
Damage per second — both the stat and the team role whose whole job is dealing damage (vs. tank and healer).
terms.example: “We have two healers, we need more DPS.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: The invisible shape the game uses to decide whether an attack connects. When it’s bigger or smaller than the character looks, players riot.
terms.example: “I dodged that! The hitbox is broken.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: The current “best” strategies, characters, or loadouts the community has settled on. Playing “off-meta” means ignoring them.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Random number generation — luck, as a game mechanic. “RNG carried me” = I got lucky; “RNGesus” = the deity of drop rates.
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Downloadable content — extra maps, characters, or story sold after the base game.
terms.example: “The DLC costs almost as much as the game.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Any computer-controlled enemy that exists to be fought — short for “mobile object.” Bosses are mobs with an ego.
terms.example: “Clear the mobs before pulling the boss.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: Deliberately ruining other players’ fun within the game’s rules — destroying their builds, blocking doorways, team-killing.
terms.example: “Someone griefed our base while we were offline.”
terms.sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of video game terms

terms.definition: To understand something so deeply it becomes intuitive. From Heinlein’s “Stranger in a Strange Land,” adopted by hackers.
terms.example: “Give me a week with the codebase and I’ll grok it.”

terms.definition: A feature that makes it easy to shoot yourself in the foot — dangerous by design.
terms.example: “Editing production configs by hand is a classic footgun.”

terms.definition: An error in software that makes it behave incorrectly. Famously linked to an actual moth found in a 1947 Harvard computer.
terms.example: “It’s not a bug, it’s a feature.”

terms.definition: A problem that only appears at extreme or unusual inputs — the empty list, the year 2038, the user named “Null.”
terms.example: “Works fine until someone’s name has an apostrophe. Edge case.”

terms.definition: A bug where the outcome depends on which of two operations happens to finish first. Notoriously hard to reproduce.
terms.example: “It only fails under load — smells like a race condition.”

terms.definition: When a program keeps claiming memory and never gives it back, slowly eating the machine until something crashes.
terms.example: “The server needs a restart every night — there’s a leak somewhere.”

terms.definition: Restructuring code to make it cleaner without changing what it does. Like reorganizing the kitchen: same meals, saner drawers.
terms.example: “I refactored the auth module — same behavior, half the code.”

terms.definition: Repetitive setup code you must write over and over with little variation before the interesting part starts.
terms.example: “Half the file is just boilerplate imports and config.”

terms.definition: Old code the business still depends on but everyone is afraid to touch. Often works perfectly; nobody knows why.
The list of function calls a program prints when it crashes — the breadcrumb trail back to what went wrong.
terms.example: “Don’t describe the error, paste the stack trace.”

terms.definition: When two people edit the same lines and version control makes a human decide whose change wins. A rite of passage.
terms.example: “I lost the afternoon to a 40-file merge conflict.”

terms.definition: Copying code or rituals without understanding why they work, hoping the results follow anyway.
terms.example: “Nobody knows what that config line does; we keep it out of cargo cult.”

terms.definition: Counting one too many or one too few — the classic loop bug. The two hardest problems in CS: naming, caching, and off-by-one errors.
terms.example: “The list shows 9 items instead of 10 — off-by-one.”

terms.definition: Solving a problem in the fewest possible characters, readability be damned. A sport, not a workplace practice.
terms.example: “He code-golfed it down to 38 characters. Nobody can read it.”

terms.definition: An inelegant, duct-taped workaround that gets the job done. Pronounced “klooj.”
terms.example: “The timezone fix is a kludge, but it ships today.”

terms.definition: The way untouched software mysteriously stops working over time as everything around it changes.
terms.example: “The deploy script hit bit rot — three of its dependencies died.”

terms.definition: A tool that nags about code style and suspicious patterns before they become bugs. Named after picking lint off clothes.
terms.example: “CI failed because the linter hates my semicolons.”

terms.definition: Modifying someone else’s code at runtime without touching the source. Powerful, fragile, and frowned upon.
terms.example: “We monkey-patched the library until the fix ships upstream.”

terms.definition: One class that knows about everything and does everything. The opposite of good design; every codebase has one.
terms.example: “The User class is 4,000 lines. Total god object.”

terms.definition: A problem that keeps revealing deeper problems the further you dig. You go in to fix a typo, you emerge three days later.
terms.example: “The ‘quick fix’ turned into a rabbit hole.”

terms.definition: Best friends forever. Noun now — “she’s my bff.”
Be right there.
See ya. Goodbye.
Don’t worry.
F*** my life. Dramatic despair over minor misfortune.
For the win. Enthusiastic endorsement — gaming origin, now general.
I know, right? Emphatic agreement.
I miss you.
My face when. Pairs with a reaction image/gif; cousin of TFW.
No big deal. Often ironic humble-brag.
Not safe for work — content you shouldn’t open around others. A warning label parents should know.
terms.example: “Don’t click that at school, it’s nsfw.”

terms.definition: One of my followers/friends. Vague-posting about someone without naming them.
Rolling on the floor laughing. LOL escalation tier.
Thanks. Also “ty” (thank you) and “tysm” (thank you so much).
Too long; didn’t read. Either a confession or a label on the one-line summary of a wall of text.
You’re welcome.
Get ready with me — a video format where someone films their morning/going-out routine while chatting.
Outfit of the day. Fashion-post caption.
Experience points — the currency of leveling up. Kids apply it to life: chores are “no XP.”
terms.example: “Two more quests and I level up — need the XP.”

terms.definition: Health points / hit points. Zero HP = dead. Also used jokingly about being tired.
terms.example: “I’m at like 5 HP after that practice.”

terms.definition: Overpowered — too strong, needs a nerf. Also “original poster” in forums, context decides.
The wait before an ability can be used again. Borrowed for real life: “my social battery is on cooldown.”
Critical hit — a randomly-boosted attack that does extra damage.
When a random effect actually triggers (“programmed random occurrence”). “My lifesteal procced twice.”
Where/when something appears in the game world. Spawn point, spawn camping, respawn.
terms.example: “Enemies spawn behind the barn every wave.”

terms.definition: When death is permanent — no respawn, character gone forever. Hardcore mode.
A build with huge damage but almost no defense — devastating until anything touches it.
terms.example: “She runs full glass cannon — one hit and she’s down.”

terms.definition: Optimizing a build to maximize strengths and dump everything irrelevant. Spreadsheet-brain gaming.
terms.example: “He min-maxed his character before session one.”

terms.definition: Faking out a pursuer with sudden direction changes. From football, huge in MOBAs.
A cheat/debug mode that turns off collision so you fly through walls. Also meme shorthand for glitching out of reality.
terms.example: “Used noclip to see outside the map.”

terms.definition: Chaining jumps to move faster than intended — a physics exploit turned art form in shooters.
terms.example: “He bunny hopped across the whole map.”

terms.definition: Player versus environment — fighting computer enemies instead of humans. The chill counterpart to PvP.
terms.example: “I only queue PvE, ranked stresses me out.”

terms.definition: First-person shooter — the genre. Also frames per second, the performance stat. Same letters, both gaming.
Massively multiplayer online game — thousands of players in one persistent world.
terms.example: “He’s been in the same MMO guild for years.”

terms.definition: Multiplayer online battle arena (League of Legends, Dota 2) — 5v5 lane-pushing strategy games.
Shorthand for the trivial detail everyone has an opinion on (see bikeshedding). “What color is this bikeshed?” = we’re wasting time.
terms.example: “Tabs vs spaces is bikeshed color territory.”

terms.definition: Approving a code review without genuinely reading it. The dark side of LGTM.
The scenario where every input is valid and nothing goes wrong. Code that only handles the happy path breaks on contact with users.
terms.example: “The demo works because it only shows the happy path.”

terms.definition: Reverting to the previous version after a release goes wrong. The “undo” button of deployments.
An urgent patch shipped outside the normal release cycle to stop the bleeding. Gamers know it from emergency balance patches.
An isolated environment where code can run without hurting anything real. In gaming: a genre where you build freely (Minecraft).
terms.example: “Test it in the sandbox before it touches prod.”

terms.definition: Production — the live system real users touch. “Testing in prod” is the confession of the brave and the doomed.
terms.example: “Who pushed straight to prod on a Friday?”

terms.definition: A project quietly growing beyond its original plan, one “small addition” at a time.
terms.example: “The todo app now has a social feed. Scope creep.”

terms.definition: To check in briefly. Baseball metaphor; the unit of corporate small talk.
terms.example: “Let’s touch base Monday about the launch.”

terms.definition: An outcome claimed to benefit both sides. Sometimes even true.
To go from summary to detail — clicking into the numbers behind the numbers.
terms.example: “Let’s drill down into why churn spiked.”

terms.definition: A specific task assigned in a meeting. Meetings are judged by how few of these survive.
terms.example: “Three action items came out of standup.”

terms.definition: The industry-accepted “right way” to do something. Invoked to end arguments.
terms.example: “Code review before merge is best practice.”

terms.definition: Someone positioned as a visionary in their field. Half admiration, half eye-roll, depending on who says it.
terms.example: “He posts like a LinkedIn thought leader now.”

terms.definition: To brainstorm — but fancier. The verb form of a whiteboard session.
End of day — the classic soft deadline. “By EOD” means today, timezone negotiable.
terms.example: “Can you send the deck by EOD?”

terms.definition: Out of office. The status, the auto-reply, and the dream.
Key performance indicator — the specific numbers a team is judged by.
terms.example: “Signups are our main KPI this quarter.”

terms.definition: Return on investment — what you got back for what you put in. Demanded of every idea, including lunch.
terms.example: “What’s the ROI on sponsoring that event?”

terms.definition: A sharp change of strategy when the current one isn’t working, rebranded as vision.
terms.example: “The startup pivoted from an app to a B2B tool.”

terms.definition: Be f***ing for real. Exasperated “you can’t be serious.” Softened aloud to “be for real.”
terms.example: “You lost the permission slip again? bffr.”

terms.definition: A sharp, witty comeback to criticism — quick and public.
terms.example: “Her clapback in the comments ended him.”

terms.definition: Excellent — especially of memes: absurd, layered, deep-internet humor. Originally cannabis slang, now mostly about memes.
A self-declared life phase, Taylor Swift-style: “in my gym era,” “in my villain era.” Any mood can be an era.
Manipulating someone into doubting their own memory or sanity. Teens use it loosely for any denial: “stop gaslighting me, you DID say that.”
terms.example: “He gaslit the whole group chat about the plan.”

terms.definition: An exclamation (from “goddamn”) reacting to an attractive body, especially a butt. Parents: this one is objectifying — worth a conversation.
terms.example: Kid yells “gyat” in the hallway; teacher sighs.

terms.definition: A young kid or someone younger than you (Southern/Florida origin). Can be affectionate or dismissive.
terms.example: “The jits at the park were trying to hoop with us.”

terms.definition: Someone’s backstory — the deep personal history that explains them. From game/fandom worldbuilding: “what’s her lore?”
terms.example: “Wait, he used to be a child actor? That’s crazy lore.”

terms.definition: The ultimate compliment for a woman who dominates her field — “she’s mother.” From ballroom culture via stan Twitter.
terms.example: “Did you see her halftime show? Mother.”

terms.definition: The sound of witnessing something awkward — “and I oop.” Filler reaction to drama or a slip-up.
terms.example: “She walked in right as we were talking about her. Oop.”

terms.definition: Opposition — an enemy, rival, or hater. From drill rap; now any adversary, including your sibling who told on you.
terms.example: “Don’t invite him, he’s been moving like an opp.”

terms.definition: Proof — screenshots, photos, saved messages. “Bring the receipts” = back up your claim.
terms.example: “She denied it, so I pulled up the receipts.”

terms.definition: Shocked, rattled, emotionally destabilized. “I’m still shook.”
Hinting at a new relationship online without revealing who — a hand in one photo, a second coffee cup. The opposite of a hard launch.
terms.example: “The mystery arm in her story? Total soft launch.”

terms.definition: As soon as possible. The original urgency acronym.
Also known as.
Estimated time of arrival. “ETA?” = when will you get here?
I love you so much. ILY, escalated.
Okay — friendlier than a bare “k,” which reads as cold or annoyed. The double letter defuses it.
Love you. Quick sign-off among friends and family.
Yes — but tone matters. Can be genuine agreement or flat, skeptical “sure.”
No thank you.
Oh my lord. OMG variant.
terms.example: “oml the test got moved to today.”

terms.definition: On the way. Interchangeable with OMW.
Real quick. “Come here rq.”
Take your time.
Whatever. Often signals passive indifference — “wtv” can mean it’s fine or it’s very much not fine.
At the moment. Not the cash machine.
To be determined/decided. Placeholder for unknowns.
Something. Also smh’s easily-confused cousin — read carefully.
Seriously.
terms.example: “srsly stop leaving dishes in the sink.”

terms.definition: What do you mean?
For sure. Agreement — “fs fs” for emphasis.
Good night.
Good morning.
I don’t even know. IDK with extra bewilderment.
I don’t remember.
In my humble opinion. IMO with a bow tie.
A hidden secret developers tuck into a game (or any software) for players to discover.
terms.example: “There’s an Easter egg if you visit the lighthouse at night.”

terms.definition: Games where you spend currency on randomized character/item pulls — slot-machine mechanics, from Japanese capsule toys. Parents: this is where the money goes.
terms.example: “He spent his birthday money on gacha pulls.”

terms.definition: Heads-up display — the health bars, ammo counts, and minimaps overlaid on the screen.
terms.example: “Playing with the HUD off is hardcore mode.”

terms.definition: Swooping in for the final blow after a teammate did all the work — stealing the credit and often the reward.
terms.example: “Bro kill-stole after I got him to 1 HP.”

terms.definition: The system that pairs players of (theoretically) similar skill into matches. Blamed for every loss.
terms.example: “Matchmaking put us against a full pro squad.”

terms.definition: A game where spending real money buys competitive advantage, not just cosmetics. Said with contempt.
terms.example: “The new shop items are straight pay-to-win.”

terms.definition: The floppy physics a character’s body gets when defeated — and the hilarious glitches it produces.
terms.example: “His ragdoll flew across the whole map.”

terms.definition: Wrecked — thoroughly destroyed. “Get rekt” is the taunt.
A bad player who blames everything but their own play — worse connotation than noob, which at least implies newness.
A cosmetic outfit/appearance for a character or weapon. No gameplay effect; enormous social effect.
terms.example: “He has every rare skin in the game.”

terms.definition: Getting stuck in a game state where progress is impossible but the game hasn’t crashed — no error, just doom.
terms.example: “Saved with 0 HP outside the boss room. Softlocked.”

terms.definition: To completely miss an attack, especially an important one, especially in front of everyone.
terms.example: “He whiffed the ultimate and we lost the fight.”

terms.definition: When the entire team dies — a full party wipe. Also a fresh-start server reset in survival games.
terms.example: “One bad pull and it was a full wipe.”

terms.definition: A save point mid-level so death doesn’t send you back to the start.
terms.example: “Thank god there was a checkpoint before the boss.”

terms.definition: A chained sequence of attacks executed without a break. The bread and butter of fighting games.
To kill something in a single hit — or be killed in one. “The boss one-shots you if you miss the dodge.”
A game you can roam freely instead of following fixed levels — go anywhere, ignore the story, pet the dog.
terms.example: “100 hours in and I haven’t touched the main quest. Open world things.”

terms.definition: Hostile, insulting behavior in games and communities — flaming, blaming, slurs. The catch-all word for bad online behavior.
An update that fixes bugs and rebalances the game. “Patch notes” are required reading; “patched out” = the fun exploit is gone.
The traditional first program in any language: print “Hello, world!” The programmer’s first step since the 1970s.
terms.example: “Day one of learning Rust: hello world compiles.”

terms.definition: Language features that make code sweeter to write but add no new power — a nicer way to say the same thing.
“If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it’s a duck” — caring what an object can do, not what it’s called.
terms.example: “Python doesn’t check the type — duck typing.”

terms.definition: A brand-new project with no legacy constraints — the developer’s dream. Opposite: brownfield.
terms.example: “It’s a greenfield build, we can pick any stack.”

terms.definition: A period before release when no new changes are allowed — only critical fixes. Always announced; always violated.
terms.example: “We’re in code freeze until the launch.”

terms.definition: A quick “does it even turn on?” check before deeper testing — from hardware, where the first test is whether it smokes.
terms.example: “Smoke test passed, running the full suite now.”

terms.definition: Software announced with fanfare that never actually ships. Gamers know the pain.
terms.example: “That sequel has been vaporware for a decade.”

terms.definition: Poor quality; stuttery, unreliable, held together with tape. “Janky” describes half the internet.
terms.example: “The animation is janky on older phones.”

terms.definition: Two developers, one keyboard: one types, one navigates. Half code review, half buddy system.
Presenting a problem so interesting that the victim drops everything to solve it. From xkcd #356.
terms.example: “The puzzle nerd-sniped the whole engineering channel.”

terms.definition: Scope creep’s product cousin: features piling onto a product until it collapses under its own settings menu.
terms.example: “The app has 9 toolbars now. Feature creep won.”

terms.definition: A rough estimate. “Give me a ballpark” = I won’t hold you to it (they will).
Where projects go to be “not cancelled” — deprioritized indefinitely.
terms.example: “The rebrand is on the back burner until Q3.”

terms.definition: To follow up and finish an open conversation so everyone has the final answer.
terms.example: “Closing the loop: the vendor confirmed Friday.”

terms.definition: The concrete thing you owe: the report, the deck, the build. Work, but nounified.
terms.example: “What are the deliverables for phase one?”

terms.definition: Getting organized before acting — everything prepared and lined up.
terms.example: “Let’s get our ducks in a row before the client call.”
terms.sourceName: Wiktionary — get one's ducks in a row

terms.definition: Trying to coordinate people who refuse to be coordinated. Every group project ever.
The single guiding goal or metric everything else should serve.
A team that doesn’t share information with others. “Breaking down silos” is the eternal reorg promise.
Anyone with a stake in the outcome — the people who must be kept happy, informed, or at least quiet.
terms.example: “Loop in the stakeholders before we commit.”

terms.definition: The bare minimum required to even compete — from poker’s minimum buy-in.
terms.example: “Mobile support isn’t a feature anymore, it’s table stakes.”

terms.definition: Publicly blaming a colleague to save yourself.
terms.example: “He threw the whole design team under the bus in the retro.”

terms.definition: The extra benefit something brings — or a buzzword prefix for anything a vendor wants to charge more for.
terms.example: “What’s the value-add of the premium tier?”

terms.definition: As a verb: to estimate roughly. “Ballpark it for me.”
Living “rent free in your head” = you can’t stop thinking about someone/something, and they aren’t even paying for the space. Teens use it as a taunt.
terms.example: “You’re still mad about that game? It’s living rent free.”

terms.definition: Corporate for “I already told you this — read it this time.” The politest available aggression.
terms.example: “Per my last email, the deadline was Tuesday.”

terms.definition: “Kill myself.” Sometimes dark humor over small failures — but always worth taking seriously and checking in. Bark flags this as a self-harm signal.
terms.example: “I failed my test, I’m going to KMS.”

terms.definition: “Kill yourself.” Used as a vicious insult or cyberbullying. Never dismiss it — sent or received.
terms.example: Seen in hostile game chats and bullying messages.

terms.definition: Blackmail using intimate images: a predator (often posing as a peer) convinces a teen to share photos, then threatens to publish them unless paid. A fast-growing crime targeting teen boys especially.
terms.example: The FBI issues repeated warnings on teen sextortion schemes.

terms.definition: An adult building trust with a minor (gifts, secrets, flattery, “only I understand you”) to enable abuse. Often starts in games or DMs.
terms.example: Secret adult “friends” online are a classic grooming sign.

terms.definition: Someone using a fake identity/photos online, often to lure someone into a relationship or scam. Also a verb: “he got catfished.”
terms.example: “Her online boyfriend refused to video call. Total catfish.”

terms.definition: Publishing someone’s private info (address, school, phone) online to intimidate them. Also spelled dox.
terms.example: “They doxxed her after the argument went viral.”

terms.definition: Making a fake emergency call to send armed police to someone’s home. A “prank” with lethal history, often aimed at streamers.
terms.example: Streamers have been swatted live on camera.

terms.definition: Bullying through phones and social platforms: harassment, exclusion, rumor-spreading, or account pile-ons. Follows kids home in their pocket.
terms.example: Group-chat pile-ons are the modern lunchroom bullying.

terms.definition: Another name for a secondary/fake social account where kids post freely, away from adult eyes.
terms.example: “I have a spam where I post whatever.”

terms.definition: A hand-me-down or traded phone kids keep secret — used for internet access after their main phone is confiscated. Wi-Fi is all it needs.
terms.example: “They took his phone so he got a trap phone.”

terms.definition: A secret meetup, usually romantic/sexual, kept hidden from parents and sometimes friends. The person is also called your sneaky link.
terms.example: “She left at midnight for a sneaky link.”

terms.definition: The number of people someone has slept with. Common in teen banter — worth knowing what’s actually being discussed.
A deliberately provocative selfie posted to harvest attention and compliments.
terms.example: “That gym mirror pic is a thirst trap.”

terms.definition: “Down to f***” — looking for casual sex.
terms.example: Appears in dating-app bios and DMs.

terms.definition: Friends with benefits — friends who hook up without commitment.
“F*** boy” — a guy pursuing sex with no intention of commitment.
terms.example: “He’s a total fboi, don’t text back.”

terms.definition: To have casual sex. “Smash or pass” is the rating game.
“Come over to watch a movie” — where the movie is not the point. Euphemism for hooking up.
terms.example: “Wanna Netflix and chill?” is rarely about the show.

terms.definition: “Talk dirty to me.” A sexting acronym.
Usually “like my pic” — but Bark notes it can also stand for a sexual phrase. Context matters.
“Age/sex/location” — the classic stranger-chat opener, still used. A stranger asking your kid’s ASL is a red flag.
“Where you from?” — location-probing from online strangers.
A drug dealer or source — someone who can “connect” you. “My plug” can also be used jokingly for any hookup (shoes, tickets).
A drink of codeine cough syrup mixed with soda/candy. Also called purple drank or sizzurp. Glamorized in some rap culture.
terms.example: References to “pouring up” or purple cups signal lean.

terms.definition: High-grade (“exotic”) marijuana.
Triple meaning: marijuana, something cool (“that song is gas”), or hyping someone up (“gas me up”). Context decides.
terms.example: “That’s gas” may or may not be about weed.

terms.definition: Marijuana reference — April 20 is the informal weed holiday, 4:20 the time.
Inhaling concentrated cannabis (“dabs”) — much stronger than flower. Also, separately, the old arm-fold dance move.
terms.example: “He was dabbing at the party” — check context.

terms.definition: A small, discreet e-cigarette resembling a USB drive; “pods” are the nicotine cartridges. Shorthand for vaping generally.
Slang for a green 2mg benzodiazepine bar (counterfeit pills are common and dangerous). Named for the color.
Slang for a yellow 2mg Xanax bar. Innocent-sounding words hiding pill talk is the pattern to know.
terms.example: “He ate a school bus” is not about transportation.

terms.definition: “That ho over there” — a slut-shaming insult. Hearing your kid use or receive it is conversation-worthy.
terms.example: Used like “slut” in insults and gossip.

terms.definition: “Shut the f*** up.” Ranges from playful disbelief (“no way!”) to genuine hostility.
terms.example: “I got tickets!” “STFU!!” — or aimed at someone, bullying.

terms.definition: “Shut your b**** a** up.” A harsher STFU, common in comment-section fights.
Short form of “b****.” Casual among friends or an insult — tone decides.
Body-shaming slang mocking someone’s size or appetite. Often “joking” — frequently bullying.
terms.example: “Stop calling people big back for eating seconds.”

terms.definition: Graphic anime pornography. Easily stumbled into via anime-adjacent searches.
terms.example: A search-history term parents should recognize.

terms.definition: Explicit acronym from the Cardi B / Megan Thee Stallion song — sexual meaning, mainstream exposure.
terms.example: Kids quote the song; the acronym is explicit.

terms.definition: To ejaculate. Slipped into songs and jokes; parents rarely catch it.
terms.example: Heard in lyrics and locker-room jokes.

terms.definition: Slang for penis (one of many food-word stand-ins).
Slang for penis — while also being a real tech word for a small adapter, which is exactly why kids find it funny.
“Downlow trade” — someone quietly gay/queer who isn’t easily perceived as LGBTQ+. Outing-adjacent gossip term.
terms.example: “They’re giving dl trade” speculates on someone’s sexuality.

terms.definition: Consecutive days of Snapchat exchanges with a friend. Streaks create real social pressure — kids share passwords to keep them alive on vacation.
Penis. The most famous coded emoji — never about cooking.
Butt. Almost never the fruit.
terms.example: Thirst-trap comments are full of these.

terms.definition: Ejaculation / sexual arousal in flirty contexts. (Sometimes literally sweat or water — context.)
terms.example: Paired with 🍑 or 🍆 the meaning is clear.

terms.definition: Sexual activity, especially oral sex, in flirty exchanges.
Oral sex — “giving brain.” One parents almost never catch.
terms.example: Not about studying in flirty chats.

terms.definition: “Porn” — corn rhymes and dodges content filters, especially on TikTok (“corn industry”).
Nudes — “noods.” Pasta as camouflage.
General “interested/watching”... but Bark notes it’s also used when sending or requesting nudes. Context matters a lot.
terms.example: Innocent in group chats; loaded in DMs.

terms.definition: Vagina. Another food stand-in.
terms.example: Flirty contexts only — otherwise it’s lunch.

terms.definition: Breasts, testicles, or virginity depending on context.
terms.example: Loaded in flirty bios and comments.

terms.definition: “You’re hot” — sexual attraction. Standard crush-selfie comment.
Feeling frisky or naughty — flirty mischief with sexual undertones.
Desiring someone sexually; Bark notes it’s often a response to nudes.
Sexual activity (“smashing”). Not about home repair in DMs.
A large, shapely butt — “dump truck” is the compliment.
An “hourglass” body shape compliment.
Marijuana. The polite little breeze emoji is the weed emoji.
Drunkenness, sexual arousal, or a general grimace — Bark lists all three.
“I’m dead” = that’s hilarious. The modern crying-laughing emoji. Not morbid.
A lie — visual form of “cap.” Reply 🧢 to call someone out.
Being ghosted — dumped or dropped with zero explanation.
Self-mockery or an insult: caught in a mistake, played yourself, acted a fool.
Suppressed annoyance or ironic “everything is fine.” The passive-aggressive smiley.
terms.example: “Group project due tomorrow and no one started 🙃”

terms.definition: Response to a savage comment — “that was cold.”
Shy, nervous, bashful — usually while flirting or asking for something.
The nazar amulet — warding off bad vibes and jealousy. Spiritual protection aesthetic.
terms.example: In bios next to birth year.

terms.definition: Stunned, awkward witnessing — “it is what it is.” Pure absurdist reaction meme.
Marks a sarcastic, sweetly-mean comment — “fairy comment” culture: cruelty delivered in glitter.
“Take my money” — wanting something badly in a video, TikTok comment-section currency.
Full agreement, approval, “facts.” The stamp of authenticity.
“Spicy” — risqué or inappropriate content warning/label.
terms.example: “The 🌶️ version is on her other account.”

terms.definition: Sadness or disappointment with a comedic, dramatic-emo flavor.
From the Vine “what’s 9+10?” “21!” — the wrong answer as a running joke. Say 9+10 near a kid and wait.
A deeply relatable feeling or situation. Often just “mood.”
terms.example: “Skipping plans to stay in bed? A mood.”

terms.definition: Caps a statement as final truth: “and that’s on periodt,” “and that’s on everything.”
terms.example: “I’m passing this class, and that’s on everything.”

terms.definition: Significant other or crush (“before anyone else”).
Weak, submissive, a follower — the insult opposite of alpha/sigma in the male-hierarchy meme taxonomy.
The dominant-leader personality in the same meme taxonomy as sigma and beta. Often used ironically now.
terms.example: “He thinks he’s the alpha of the friend group.”

terms.definition: The Charli XCX “Brat” aesthetic: messy-cool partying, lime green, unapologetic confidence.
“Bro,” but mostly an exasperated reaction to anything. The all-purpose deadpan.
terms.example: “Bruh. You did NOT just say that.”

terms.definition: “Be so for real” — disbelief, “are you serious right now?” Sibling of bffr.
Bad quality, trash. “That movie was buns.”
A large butt. Food-compliment family with “thicc.”
Bad quality — same slot as “buns.”
The definitive representative of a behavior: “CEO of being late.”
terms.example: “Taylor is the CEO of sleeping in.”

terms.definition: Jokingly big, chunky, over-the-top. From the Big Chungus Bugs Bunny meme.
“Chopped huzz” — unattractive people, in the ever-expanding -uzz family (huzz, bruzz, gruzz, chuzz).
Unsettling, creepy, wrong — usually about disturbing images. Opposite of “blessed.”
Secondhand embarrassment as an adjective. The ultimate teen dismissal.
terms.example: “Dad dancing at the party was so cringe.”
