terms.definition: A Division-1-athlete-level crash out — an elite, certifiable meltdown.
terms.example: “She had a D1 crash out over the group chat.”

terms.definition: An attractive, usually older man projecting power/dominance. Yes, it’s weird for parents to hear.
terms.example: “Why is the new teacher kind of daddy?” — conversation time.

terms.definition: Deliberate misspelling of “dead” = that’s hilarious. Skull emoji in word form.
Modest, mindful — turned 2024 meme aesthetic (“very demure, very mindful”). Ironic elegance.
Take the risk — life is a story and this is character development, even if it goes badly.
terms.example: “Trying out even if I flop. Doing it for the plot.”

terms.definition: Leaning all the way into pessimism as an identity. The -maxxing suffix (from looksmaxxing) applied to despair.
Cool, awesome. A classic that never fully left.
A young person with emo/punk-inspired internet style — chains, stripes, dyed hair, heavy eyeliner.
Facial attractiveness as a bank card: “her face card never declines” = flawlessly pretty, always.
terms.example: “Woke up like that. Face card never declines.”

terms.definition: “Fine as sh**” — a very attractive person. The respelling keeps it filter-safe.
From a viral video of a student ranting that the teacher just “handed us a friggin’ packet yo” instead of teaching. Now the cry of every worksheet-weary kid.
terms.example: “Sub just gave us a friggin’ packet.”

terms.definition: Cut off with zero explanation — no reply, no goodbye, just gone.
terms.example: “Three dates and then he ghosted me.”

terms.definition: Aspirational — something you want for yourself. “Couple goals,” “hair goals.”
Old people, in the -uzz family. Grandma’s bridge club = the gruzz.
Good, fine, all set. “We’re Gucci” = no problems here.
Openly, very much — the loud opposite of low key.
terms.example: “I high key want pizza right now.”

terms.definition: Somewhat, quietly, or keep-it-secret. “Low key stressed” = admitting it softly.
From a viral video: a kid draws mom with a dot on her face; mom asks “is that hyperpigmentation?” Now a nonsense meme word kids deploy randomly.
In search of. Marketplace-post shorthand.
An entitled, manager-demanding middle-aged woman. The archetype of privileged public meltdowns.
terms.example: “She went full Karen at the drive-thru.”

terms.definition: Did it perfectly — the completion of “ate.” Nothing left to criticize.
terms.example: “She ate that speech and left no crumbs.”

terms.definition: Go 100%, full send. The modern YOLO, from extreme-sports culture.
terms.example: “Last day of finals — let’s get sendy.”

terms.definition: Exciting, popular, going off. Can also mean intoxicated — context.
Someone extremely attractive — beyond snack. “He’s a whole meal.”
A young person with boomer attitudes — the insult for kids who complain like it’s 1965.
terms.example: “He hates all new music. Total neoboomer.”

terms.definition: The best possible version of something — “peak fiction,” “peak Fortnite era.” (In UK slang it can mean bad — context.)
The updated preppy aesthetic: bright girly colors, Lululemon, Stanley cups. More brand-forward than the old money version.
“I relate completely.” A full sentence.
Gossiping about someone without naming them — throwing shade with plausible deniability.
terms.example: “That post is definitely shading her ex.”

terms.definition: To root for two people to be together — “I ship them.” From “relationship,” born in fandom.
“Sister” — address for anyone, usually signaling incoming drama or realness.
terms.example: “Sis, sit down, you need to hear this.”

terms.definition: The surreal animated YouTube series of singing toilet heads that birthed “skibidi.” It is not supposed to make sense. Gen Alpha’s Peanut Butter Jelly Time.
terms.example: Your 8-year-old singing at the dinner table: this is why.

terms.definition: Avoiding someone in real life without confrontation — the offline version of quietly blocking.
terms.example: “I’m soft-blocking him IRL, it’s too awkward.”

terms.definition: Rapid, emotional posting during distress. A visible cry for help worth checking on, not mocking.
terms.example: “She was spiral posting at 3am — I called to check in.”

terms.definition: The close friend group. “Squad goals” = friendship aspirations.
To pick someone up in a car. “I’ll swoop you at 8.”
Attractively curvy. The extra c’s are the compliment.
terms.example: “The gym is working, you’re thicc now.”

terms.definition: Desperate for attention, usually romantic/sexual. The thirst trap is its instrument.
Terrible. Applied to games, teams, takes, and cafeteria food.
“Very.” Single-letter efficiency: “that’s v cool.”
Relaxing, enjoying the moment, in sync with the energy. No agenda, just vibes.
terms.example: “We were just vibing to music all night.”

terms.definition: Socially/politically conscious. Now heavily politicized — praise or insult depending entirely on the speaker.
terms.example: “The movie got called woke by half the internet.”

terms.definition: An extremely emphatic yes. More A’s = more enthusiasm.
To throw something with force — or an exclamation of doing anything energetically. Past tense: yote (jokingly).
terms.example: “He yeeted his backpack across the room.”

terms.definition: A stylish, attractive man of any age — daddy with fashion sense.
terms.example: “Since the makeover he’s a whole zaddy.”

terms.definition: A hyper-confident, conventionally masculine alpha guy. Both mocking and (in “gigachad”) genuine praise.
terms.example: “He asked her out in front of everyone. Chad move.”

terms.definition: Relaxed, easygoing — person or plan. “We’re chill” = no conflict.
Cardi B’s trilled “okay” — said when someone gets put in their place, or as celebration.
“High Expectations Asian Father” — a meme archetype about intense academic pressure.
terms.example: “My dad is such a HEAF about grades.”

terms.definition: The wish-making time. Kids text “11:11” with their wish or crush initials.
The K-pop juggernaut boy band. Knowing the name buys parent credibility; confusing them with another group destroys it.
Someone overly eager/obsessed with pleasing another person (Ice Spice popularized it; has sexual undertones).
terms.example: “He does everything she says — total munch.”

terms.definition: Extremely excited/hyped — or high, depending on context.
To dance hard — “get sturdy” is the NY drill dance style. Also general hype.
The straight-across-fringe haircut popular with young Latino men — and the teasing name for guys who wear it.
terms.example: “Every kid at the mall has an edgar now.”

terms.definition: Japanese for “idiot” — imported by anime fans as a (usually) playful insult.
To crave something obsessively (from “fiend,” boosted by Travis Scott’s “FE!N”). Spelled fein or feen.
As f*** — intensifier. “Tired af.”
Shaking my damn head — SMH with feeling.
Rolling on the floor laughing my a** off. The maximal laugh acronym.
What the f***. Shock, confusion, outrage.
“The f***” — attached anywhere for emphasis: “who tf,” “why tf.”
What’s good? Greeting.
What’s the word? / What’s the wave? — asking what’s happening tonight.
Swear to God — ISTG minus the I.
How are you?
“I guess” — reluctant agreement. (Also Instagram — context.)
For f***’s sake. Exasperation.
What’s up?
Yeah.
Really.
Please. Also “pls.”
Great — the number-substitution classic (gr8, l8r, m8, b4).
Before.
Your / you’re. The apostrophe’s natural predator.
Competitive gaming as organized sport — leagues, teams, arenas, scholarships, real salaries.
Someone who broadcasts themselves gaming (or just living) live on Twitch/YouTube. A dream job for a generation.
terms.example: “She wants to be a streamer when she grows up.”

terms.definition: The dominant live-streaming platform for gaming. Chat culture there birthed poggers, KEKW, and half of internet slang.
A streamer who appears as an animated avatar instead of their real face — a huge scene from Japan, now global.
terms.example: “Her favorite streamer is a VTuber fox girl.”

terms.definition: A character animation (dances, taunts) or a chat reaction image. Fortnite dances are emotes; kids buy them with real money.
terms.example: “He hit the emote after the win.”

terms.definition: A seasonal paid reward track — play to unlock skins/emotes tier by tier. Engineered to keep kids playing daily so the purchase doesn’t “go to waste.”
terms.example: “He grinds nightly to finish the battle pass.”

terms.definition: Small in-game purchases — skins, currency, passes. Individually tiny; collectively how “free” games make billions.
terms.example: “The game is free but the microtransactions add up fast.”

terms.definition: Playing together across different consoles/PC. Why your kid on Xbox squads with a friend on PlayStation.
terms.example: “The game has crossplay so everyone can join.”

terms.definition: The pre-match waiting area where players gather. “The lobby” is also the set of opponents: “this lobby is sweaty.”
An organized player group with a name and tag. Clan membership is real social currency.
terms.example: “He finally got recruited to that clan.”

terms.definition: The MMO version of a clan — persistent player communities with ranks, banks, and drama.
A large group challenge (MMO bosses) — or, on Twitch, sending your viewers to another channel. Also “raiding” someone’s stream/server.
An enclosed challenge area with enemies and a boss, usually run by a small party for loot.
Excellent, hype-worthy — the compact form of poggers, from Twitch’s PogChamp emote.
The set of technologies a product is built on — languages, frameworks, databases. Developers judge each other’s stacks like cars.
terms.example: “Their stack is React, Node, and Postgres.”

terms.definition: Working across both frontend and backend. The “full stack developer” does (allegedly) everything.
The part of software users see and touch — the interface. Where “it looks weird on my phone” bugs live.
The behind-the-scenes machinery — servers, databases, logic. Invisible when it works; very visible when it doesn’t.
Application programming interface — the contract that lets one program talk to another. The plumbing of the modern internet.
terms.example: “The weather app pulls from a forecast API.”

terms.definition: The culture/role merging development and operations — building, deploying, and keeping systems alive. The infinity-loop diagram people.
The iterative development philosophy — short cycles, constant feedback, embracing change. In practice: many meetings named after rugby.
terms.example: “We’re Agile now, so everything is a sprint.”

terms.definition: The most common Agile framework — sprints, standups, retros, and a “scrum master” refereeing it all.
terms.example: “Scrum says we demo every two weeks.”

terms.definition: A fixed work cycle (usually two weeks) with committed goals. Named for speed; feels like a marathon.
The short daily sync — what you did, what you’ll do, what’s blocking you. Standing optional, brevity theoretical.
The prioritized list of everything not being worked on yet. Where feature requests go to wait (sometimes forever).
Building within an existing legacy system — the constrained opposite of greenfield.
terms.example: “It’s a brownfield project, so we inherit all the old APIs.”

terms.definition: An event where everyone hammers the product at once trying to break it before release.
terms.example: “Pre-launch bug bash on Friday, all hands.”

terms.definition: Minimum viable product — the smallest version worth shipping to learn from real users. (Not the sports MVP — context.)
A whole-company meeting. Announcements, slides, forced applause.
terms.example: “They announced the merger at all hands.”

terms.definition: A single-page summary of an idea or plan — the ticket to getting leadership to read anything.
terms.example: “Send me a one-pager before the review.”

terms.definition: A rough first-draft proposal built to be torn apart and improved — “here’s a strawman to react to.”
terms.example: “I’ll bring a strawman plan to kick off discussion.”

terms.definition: How many months a startup can survive before the money runs out.
How fast a company spends its cash. High burn + short runway = layoffs incoming.
terms.example: “The new office doubled our burn rate.”

terms.definition: A private startup valued at $1B+. Rare by definition, less rare by hype.
terms.example: “Their app became a unicorn in three years.”

terms.definition: People, as a budget line. “We got headcount” = we’re allowed to hire someone.
terms.example: “No headcount for that team this year.”

terms.definition: The process of integrating a new hire (or new user) — accounts, training, culture. Its dark twin is offboarding.
Secretly removing a condom during sex without consent — a form of sexual assault. Axis includes it so parents know the word if it comes up.
terms.example: A term from conversations about consent.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Deliberately vague — anything from kissing to sex. The ambiguity is the point; ask before assuming either extreme.
terms.example: “They hooked up at the party” could mean many things.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Two meanings: a catchy song (“this song is a bop”) — or, per Axis, a derogatory term for a promiscuous girl. Context is everything.
terms.example: “That track is a bop” vs. an insult — listen carefully.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A crude suffix (from a vulgar word) teens attach to anything for shock humor. Mostly absurdist joking, but explicitly sexual in origin.
terms.example: Attached to random words for shock laughs.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Doling out just enough attention to keep someone interested without ever committing. Romantic manipulation; Axis also logs the joke name “Hansel and Gretelling.”
terms.example: “He texts her once a week — pure breadcrumbing.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A romantic interest who ghosts you… then comes back from the dead months later like nothing happened.
terms.example: “He zombied me with a ‘hey stranger’ text.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: To develop romantic feelings, often unplanned and mildly unwelcome.
terms.example: “It was casual until someone caught feels.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: To reject someone romantically — dodge their advance like a curve around an obstacle.
terms.example: “He asked for her number and got curved.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Successfully attracting romantic attention. “Who did he pull?” = who did he get.
terms.example: “Did you see who she pulled for prom?”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Significant other. “Boo’d up” = happily coupled.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: They read your message and simply… did not reply. The read receipt makes it official.
terms.example: “Left on read for six hours. I’m unwell.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Suggestive of being gay — often used playfully and, per Axis, “not always logically.”
terms.example: “Rain is fruity and I’m not explaining why.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: From drag culture: honey + an insult, softened into a sassy term of endearment among friends.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Completely serious, no joke. NY-flavored “for real.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: The sound of secondhand pain — what you say when there’s nothing to say.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: “I’m fully on board — no more information needed.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Making you laugh uncontrollably — sending you over the edge.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A dramatic preface for blunt truth: “I fear that color isn’t working.”
terms.example: “I fear the group project is doomed.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Upset, bothered, unable to let it go.
terms.example: “She’s still pressed about losing that game.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Completely over it — a person, task, or situation. Emotional resignation as a full sentence.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: “Rest in peace,” pronounced “rip” — comic despair over minor tragedy.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Acting irrational or overreacting — behavior that doesn’t make sense. From drug-influenced behavior, now general.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Shocking, unbelievable — or, of a person, acting out of pocket.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Sarcastic response to a brag about something not worth bragging about.
terms.example: “I’ve never washed my car.” “Weird flex but ok.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: The original that everyone else copies — so good it became the standard.
terms.example: “Every boy band is chasing One Direction. They’re the blueprint.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Looking exceptionally good — delivering excellence. Cousin of “ate.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Don’t interrupt — they’re mid-brilliance and the result will be impressive. Past tense: “they cooked.”
terms.example: “Wait, let him cook, this idea is actually good.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Permission to rant — or ironic “sure, do your thing.”
terms.example: “He was so rude to you. Go off!”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Stay authentic and honest — 100% real.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Really good — food edition. Sibling of “slaps.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: An attractive person. Escalates to “whole meal.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A dramatic transformation for the better — usually appearance, sometimes life.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: The culturally “ideal” hourglass body type — small waist, curves elsewhere. Worth discussing the body-image pressure it carries.
terms.example: A body-type label all over fitness TikTok.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A cohesive vibe or visual identity — noun and adjective. “That’s so aesthetic” = pleasingly styled.
terms.example: “Her room is a whole cottagecore aesthetic.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Suffixes for categorizing vibes: “cottagecore,” “2000s-core,” “Gilmore Girls-coded.” Anything can be a genre.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Feeling emotional (usually sad) — or the music/fashion subculture that never really died.
terms.example: “That movie ending has me so emo.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Outfit. “Fit check” = show us what you’re wearing. (In the UK it means attractive.)
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Car — especially a nice one.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Doing grown-up tasks (taxes, laundry, appointments) — announced with weary pride.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Plain, boring, unadventurous — basic’s blander cousin.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Alt spelling of bougie — fancy, high-class, extra.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Deliberate misspelling of “boy” — often in memes (“h boi”).
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: “About to.” Contraction of a contraction.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: “Baby/babe” — said “bee bee,” mostly between friends.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Your personal theory about fictional characters that isn’t official canon — but should be.
terms.example: “My headcanon is that Thor loves cats.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: To publicly drop someone/something as problematic. Ranges from serious accountability to joke (“you like pineapple pizza? canceled”).
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Calling someone out online without naming or tagging them — deniable public shade.
terms.example: “That post is 100% a subtweet about her ex.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Exposing someone’s embarrassing business publicly.
terms.example: “She put the group chat on blast.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Mercilessly mocked or criticized, usually publicly online.
terms.example: “The comments dragged him for that take.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A plea for engagement on your newest post. Related: LB (like back), FB (follow back). Widely seen as thirsty.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: The topic you inexplicably think about all the time — from the trend discovering men think about Rome weekly.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Uncanny, alarming, or horrifying — from art of “biblically accurate angels” (many wings, hundreds of eyes).
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: The internet’s taxonomy of images: blessed = wholesome; cursed = deeply wrong. Axis logs “cursed” for bad-luck vibes too.
terms.example: “This image is either cursed or blessed and I can’t tell.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: “I’d like to be excluded from this narrative” — Taylor Swift’s line, now shorthand for refusing involvement in drama.
terms.example: “Whatever this fight is, exclude me from the narrative.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Videos of soft sounds (whispering, tapping) meant to trigger relaxing tingles. A massive video genre kids fall asleep to.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Per Axis: “in game life” — gamers referring to their in-game world. (In esports it also means “in-game leader.”)
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: “If you know what I mean” — the winking acronym.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Hustle battle cry — bread/dough = money. Ironic-motivational.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: An intensifier prefix: big mad = furious, big sad = very sad, big brain = genius (often ironic).
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Abbreviated profanity (“god d***”) used as an intensifier in text.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Short for a crude word for penis. Parents should recognize it in “she just wants the D.”
terms.example: Single letters can carry meaning — context.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Hyping someone up — inflating their confidence.
terms.example: “Always gassing up my friends before games.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Destroyed in a match — or, harshly, ugly. Both senses common.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Accept the loss with (some) grace. Opposite: “that’s a W” (pronounced dub).
terms.example: “Wrong answer in front of everyone. Take the L.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Homecoming — the dance, the game, the proposals (“hoco proposals” are a whole genre).
terms.example: “Did you see how he asked her to hoco?”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Mind your own business; back off.
terms.example: “Why are you in my comments? Hop off.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Watch the drama without getting involved — spectate, don’t participate.
terms.example: “Not my fight. I’m just sipping tea.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Being excessively over the top when it wasn’t necessary.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Anyone (of any age) with out-of-date takes or media taste. The generational dismissal, detached from actual generations.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: So amazed your wig flew off — from drag culture. “Wig snatched” = completely blown away.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Something so good it makes you feel alive: “I’m living for this.”
terms.example: “Beach week with the squad — I’m LIVING.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: “Mental breakdown,” cutely abbreviated (via Love Island). Usually joking — but worth an ear if it isn’t.
terms.example: “One more deadline and it’s a full menty b.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Crude acronym for effortless, unbothered confidence (the kind that doesn’t need to prove anything). Explicit origin, mainstream usage.
terms.example: “He walked in like he owned it. BDE.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Objectifying slang: a “body” is someone you’ve been intimate with (see body count); “that’s a body” sexualizes a sweet gesture.
terms.example: “He made her a 4-hour playlist.” “That’s a body.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Over the top, excessive, dramatic — more than the situation required.
terms.example: “A limo for a study session? So extra.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: A (usually joking) threat to fight: “you boutta catch these hands.”
terms.example: “Talk about my team again and catch these hands.”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

terms.definition: Hyped up, wild, energetic — “turnt up.” Bark notes it can also mean drunk/stoned; context matters.
terms.example: “The crowd was turnt after that touchdown.”

terms.definition: The scrunchies-Hydro-Flask-Crocs aesthetic named after the VSCO photo app. Dated now, but still referenced.
terms.example: “Full VSCO girl energy with that water bottle.”

terms.definition: “Sh** happens.” Casual consolation. (In self-harm contexts SH can mean self-harm — context worth watching.)
AI-generated fake video/audio of a real person. Teens encounter it as manipulated clips of classmates or celebrities — increasingly used in bullying and scams.
terms.example: A “video” of a classmate that never happened.

terms.definition: AI tools that fabricate nude images from an ordinary clothed photo. Used in sextortion and school harassment cases; possessing/creating such images of minors is a crime in many places. The #1 new threat parents should know.
terms.example: A yearbook photo run through an app becomes blackmail material.

terms.definition: A long-con scam: the scammer builds a fake friendship/romance over weeks (“fattening the pig”), then lures the victim into fake crypto investments. Now targets teens and young adults on social apps.
terms.example: A friendly stranger DM that slowly turns to “investment tips.”

terms.definition: Fake online relationship built to extract money or images. The teen version often precedes sextortion.
terms.example: “My online girlfriend needs gift cards” is not a girlfriend.

terms.definition: Chatbot “friends/partners” (Character.AI-style) teens can bond with. Concerns: emotional dependence, adult content, and displacement of real relationships. Worth knowing which apps your kid talks to.
terms.example: “He spends hours talking to his AI girlfriend.”

terms.definition: Nicotine pouch brand — smokeless, spitless, easy to hide in a lip. The post-vape nicotine wave among teen boys; “zynfluencers” push it online.
terms.example: Small round tins in a backpack are worth a look.

terms.definition: Flavored nitrous oxide canisters (whipped-cream chargers) inhaled for a high — a viral 2024–25 trend. Oxygen deprivation and nerve damage are real risks.
terms.example: Colorful canisters marketed like candy on TikTok.

terms.definition: Inhaling nitrous oxide from whipped-cream chargers. Old drug, new packaging (see galaxy gas).
terms.example: Empty metal chargers in a car or room.

terms.definition: Inhaling aerosols/solvents (deodorant, paint) for a high — the TikTok-era name for huffing. Has killed kids; several viral “challenge” waves.
terms.example: Empty aerosol cans + dizzy spells = talk now.

terms.definition: “Blackout rage gallon” — a gallon jug of water, vodka, and electrolyte mix, individually carried at college parties. Framed as “safer drinking,” often just a lot of vodka.
terms.example: Gallon jugs with joke names at a tailgate.

terms.definition: “Gas-station heroin” — an opioid-like antidepressant sold in gas stations as a supplement (Neptune’s Fix, ZaZa Red). FDA-warned, addictive, and legal-ish in some states.
terms.example: Tiny red bottles from the gas station counter.

terms.definition: Fentanyl — the synthetic opioid behind most teen overdose deaths, usually hidden in counterfeit pills (“percs,” “blues”). One pill can kill; kids buying any pill online are at risk.
terms.example: “Perc 30s” from Snapchat are almost never real oxycodone.

terms.definition: Xylazine — an animal tranquilizer cut into street fentanyl (“tranq dope”). Causes wounds and doesn’t respond to Narcan.
terms.example: News reports on “zombie drug” refer to this.

terms.definition: Viral dare to take massive diphenhydramine doses to hallucinate. Caused teen deaths; resurfaces periodically on TikTok.
Eating an extremely hot pepper chip (Paqui) on camera. Sent kids to hospitals; linked to a Massachusetts teen death in 2023 and pulled from shelves — copycats persist.
terms.example: A single chip in a coffin-shaped box.

terms.definition: A live-action elimination game seniors play with water guns — harmless in theory, but police warn about realistic-looking blasters, trespassing, and ambushes near roads.
terms.example: Kids in masks stalking a friend’s driveway at 11pm.

terms.definition: Emphatic agreement — “exactly,” “real.” Often just “ts.” (Note: “ts” also means “this” in “ts pmo.”)
A hot dog. Yes, really. From DC slang (originally a gun), now 99% about hot dogs and the joke of eating one.
Mutuals — people who follow you and you follow back. Your online circle.
terms.example: “One of my moots posted it first.”

terms.definition: Best friend — someone so close you’re “twins.” Address term: “what’s good twin.”
“Gang” — address term for a friend, like bro/twin. Texting-compressed.
Deliberately misspelled “bro.” Same energy, sillier spelling. Also “crodie” in the same family.
terms.example: “vro is NOT cooking with this fit.”

terms.definition: “Bro/homie,” from Crip-adjacent replacement of B with C — now meme-ified general slang detached from gang meaning.
“I can’t lie” — the UK-flavored tbh/ngl. Often opens a confession.
Caught off-guard, unprepared, or embarrassed — from being caught without defense, now anything from a bad photo to an ambush in a game.
The 2024 viral meme from a street interview — an onomatopoeia for spitting, with an explicit original context parents should know about. Became a general-purpose meme/soundbite.
terms.example: Kids yell it as a random meme reference.

terms.definition: “What the heck” filtered through sigma-brainrot. Pure nonsense filler from the skibidi family.
terms.example: Kid drops a pencil: “what the sigma?”

terms.definition: Unapologetically lazy, messy, self-indulgent behavior — Oxford’s 2022 Word of the Year, still in rotation for rot-day energy.
terms.example: “Full goblin mode this weekend: snacks, blanket, zero pants.”

terms.definition: The 2025 wave of absurd AI-generated characters with pseudo-Italian names (Tralalero Tralala, Ballerina Cappuccina, Bombardiro Crocodilo). Younger kids recite the lore endlessly.
terms.example: Your 8-year-old chanting “tralalero tralala” — this is why.

terms.definition: GOAT as an adjective — elite, the best. “Goated with the sauce” for emphasis.
Insanely skilled. A cracked player hits every shot.
terms.example: “The kid we matched with was cracked out of his mind.”

terms.definition: Past your prime; formerly good. Applies to players, athletes, and anyone over 25 according to teenagers.
terms.example: “He used to be a demon at this game. Washed now.”

terms.definition: Short for “difference” — declaring a skill gap decided the game. “Jungle diff” = their jungler was better. Merciless in defeat.
terms.example: “That wasn’t a close match, that was a skill diff.”

terms.definition: To single-handedly win for your team — you “carried” them. Also the person who did it. Used everywhere now (“she carried the group project”).
At a rank you didn’t earn — carried there by better players. An accusation, not a compliment.
Permanently stuck at a rank despite grinding. “Hardstuck Gold” is an identity and an insult.
The theory that low ranks trap good players because teammates are too chaotic to climb out. Debated forever; blamed always.
terms.example: “I’m not bad, I’m in Elo hell.”

terms.definition: Playing worse because you’re frustrated — the anger spiral. From poker. “Tilt queue” = queuing again while mad (never works).
terms.example: “I’m tilted, one more game.” (Famous last words.)

terms.definition: Losing a game you were winning — “we threw a 20-point lead.” Also intentionally playing badly.
terms.example: “We had the win and threw it.”

terms.definition: “Intentionally feeding” — deliberately dying to ruin the game, or (jokingly) just playing terribly.
terms.example: “He’s 0-11. Either inting or having the worst day.”

terms.definition: Dying repeatedly to the enemy, making them stronger. The cardinal team-game sin.
Cope + opium — the imaginary drug you’re “on” when refusing to accept a loss or bad news. Twitch-meme chemistry; sibling of hopium (irrational hope).
terms.example: “He says the sequel will fix everything. Pure copium.”

terms.definition: Irrational optimism, inhaled like a drug. The bull-market cousin of copium.
terms.example: “Full hopium that my team makes playoffs.”

terms.definition: Mad + balding — so angry you’re losing hair. Twitch chat’s favorite way to mock a raging streamer.
terms.example: “Chat spamming MALDING as he loses again.”

terms.definition: Sad, via the Twitch emote “Sadge.” Ironic-flavored sadness in chat speak.
Twitch-chat laughter — the KEKW emote (a laughing man’s face). “KEK” is WoW-era “LOL.” Spammed when a streamer fails.
terms.example: Chat floods KEKW as the speedrun dies.

terms.definition: On another level — succeeding where everyone else fails, implying you’re constructed from superior parts. Sincere or ironic.
terms.example: “Turned in the essay early AND aced it. Built different.”

terms.definition: Building software by describing what you want to an AI and accepting what it writes — coding on vibes, not review. Coined by Karpathy (2025); powerful, controversial, occasionally catastrophic.
terms.example: “The whole app was vibe coded in a weekend.”

terms.definition: When an AI confidently invents facts, citations, or APIs that don’t exist. The core failure mode everyone building with AI must handle.
terms.example: “The chatbot cited a court case that doesn’t exist. Classic hallucination.”

terms.definition: Crafting inputs to get better outputs from AI models — part skill, part folklore, briefly a job title.
terms.example: “Adding ‘think step by step’ is prompt engineering 101.”

terms.definition: The word-chunks AI models read and write — and the unit you pay for. “Context window” = how many tokens a model can hold at once.
terms.example: “That long doc blew past the token limit.”

terms.definition: AI that takes multi-step actions on its own (browsing, running code, booking things) rather than just answering. 2025’s biggest buzzword.
terms.example: “The agentic workflow files the ticket and emails the customer itself.”

terms.definition: Low-quality AI-generated content flooding the internet — spam articles, fake images, filler videos. The sibling of the teen glossary’s “slop.”
terms.example: “Search results are half AI slop now.”

terms.definition: The stereotype: patagonia vest, disruption talk, unearned confidence. Affectionate or scathing by context.
terms.example: “He explained my own job to me. Total tech bro.”

terms.definition: Frat-culture programmer stereotype — the gym-and-code guy. Slightly dated but still deployed.
Mandatory overtime death-marches before a deadline — notorious in game studios. “Crunch culture” is the criticism.
terms.example: “The studio crunched for six months before launch.”

terms.definition: Work from home / return to office — the acronym battlefield of post-2020 work. RTO mandates are the villain in half of LinkedIn.
Communication that doesn’t need everyone present — docs and messages instead of meetings. “Let’s handle it async” = please no meeting.
Doing exactly your job and nothing more — no hustle, no unpaid extra. Not actually quitting; the 2022 phrase that named a generation’s boundary-setting.
terms.example: “He stopped answering emails at 5:01. Quiet quitting.”

terms.definition: Management making a job so unpleasant (no raises, bad shifts, exclusion) that the employee quits “voluntarily.” The employer mirror of quiet quitting.
terms.example: “Moved off every project — that’s quiet firing.”

terms.definition: Secretly working two (or more) full-time remote jobs at once. A whole subreddit-driven movement.
terms.example: “Two laptops, two standups, twice the salary.”

terms.definition: Job postings for roles companies never intend to fill — posted to look growing, harvest resumes, or pacify overworked staff.
terms.example: “That listing has been up for 8 months. Ghost job.”

terms.definition: More title and responsibility, zero extra pay.
A woman crushing it in business — sincere in 2015, almost entirely ironic now (“gaslight, gatekeep, girlboss”).
terms.example: “She girlbossed a little too close to the sun.”

terms.definition: A device/app that fakes activity so your status stays green while you step away. Companies now scan for them; people have been fired.
terms.example: “The audit found 12 mouse jigglers in accounting.”

terms.definition: Working remotely from a vacation spot (workation) or tacking leisure onto business travel (bleisure). The remote-era travel portmanteaus.
terms.example: “Two weeks in Lisbon, laptop in the mornings.”

terms.definition: A chill, decently-paid, low-stress job (often remote) that funds your actual life — a 2023 TikTok trend reframing ambition.
terms.example: “Remote coordinator role, no overtime — total lazy girl job.”

terms.definition: Marijuana. Bark lists the whole garden: 🌿 🍁 🎄 🍃 🥦 🍀 🌴 — broccoli and Christmas trees included. Context: buying/selling talk, not salad.
Cocaine — “snow.” Bark also lists 🥥 🤧 🔑 ⛄ 🎱 🐡 as cocaine codes.
terms.example: A ❄️ in a Venmo note deserves a question.

terms.definition: Pills generally — prescription drugs, oxy, or Xanax. With 🅿️ or 🔵 it often means “percs”/“blues” (usually counterfeit fentanyl — the deadliest code on this list).
Heroin/injection drugs. Bark also lists 🐉 🐎 🎯 🤎 as heroin codes.
terms.example: Rare in teen chats — but unambiguous when present.

terms.definition: Psilocybin (“magic”) mushrooms. Sometimes literal Mario nostalgia — context decides.
Cough syrup / lean codes: 🍼 🍇 💜 🔮 — purple things reference “purple drank.”
MDMA/ecstasy — “candy.” Bark also lists ❤️⚡🤯❌ combos. Also literal candy 95% of the time; look for party context.
Crystal meth codes per Bark: 💎 🏔 💙 🧪. (💎 alone is usually just “valuable/premium” — combos matter.)
Two very different uses: Bark logs it as “stoned” in drug contexts — but in meme culture it’s a deadpan/sigma reaction face. Overwhelmingly the meme; check context.
terms.example: Under a gym video it’s deadpan cool; in a dealer chat it’s stoned.

terms.definition: An ounce (of a substance being bought/sold). Pure dealer shorthand.
The plug — a dealer or source. Pairs with the slang term; in bios it advertises “I sell.”
terms.example: 🔌 in a Snapchat bio is not about chargers.

terms.definition: In dealer posts, Bark flags 🤑 💰 💵 👑 as drug-deal advertising dressing. Innocent alone; suspicious in combos with product emojis.
terms.example: 🔌+💊+💰 in one bio tells a story.

terms.definition: Smoke — a joint, vaping, or being gone/fast. With 🔥 or 🍃 it’s smoking; alone it’s often just “zoom.”
“Gas” — high-quality weed, or being gassed (intoxicated). Also the slang compliment “that’s gas.”
terms.example: ⛽ under a music drop = praise; in a buy chat = weed.

terms.definition: Bark: high-quality drugs or being very intoxicated. Elsewhere: hype/“to the moon” (crypto, stocks, games). Heavily context-dependent.
terms.example: 🚀🚀 under a meme coin vs. in a plug’s menu.

terms.definition: A large quantity of drugs (also 🍪 “cookie”). Weight-move talk, not baking.
Penis — the eggplant’s understudy. Bark logs both.
Vagina in sexting contexts (the smirking cat). Innocent as a random cat elsewhere.
To ejaculate (“bust a nut”). One parents never catch.
terms.example: In flirty chats, 🥜 is not a snack.

terms.definition: Oral sex code per Bark’s sexting guide (the combo, not either alone).
Pornhub’s logo colors — referencing porn without words. Also “P⭐” = porn star.
terms.example: ⬛🟧 in a bio or comment = porn reference.

terms.definition: “Sex” spelled to dodge filters: S-egg-s, or written “seggs.” Core algospeak parents should recognize.
terms.example: “talking about s🥚s ed” slides past moderation.

terms.definition: Your character’s appearance in a game — customizable with features, clothes, and props. The gaming ancestor of the Bitmoji.
terms.example: “Spent an hour on my avatar before playing a minute.”

terms.definition: Building virtual items from collected materials — cloth + alcohol = first-aid kit. The core loop of Minecraft, Fortnite, and survival games.
terms.example: “Need more wood to craft the shelter.”

terms.definition: “Good game, easy” — the trash-talk version of GG, snarkily implying your opponent was no challenge. Some games auto-censor it.
terms.example: Typing “gg ez” after a close match is maximum disrespect.

terms.definition: Exploiting a bug for unfair advantage — walking through walls, duplicating items. Distinct from lag: glitching is deliberate.
terms.example: “He glitched under the map so no one could hit him.”

terms.definition: Consecutive kills without dying — many shooters award bonuses at milestones, which is why your kid can’t pause right now.
terms.example: “Don’t talk to me, I’m on a 12 killstreak.”

terms.definition: Massively multiplayer online role-playing game — persistent fantasy/sci-fi worlds with thousands of players (World of Warcraft is the classic).
terms.example: “He’s been in the same MMORPG guild since middle school.”

terms.definition: A player-made modification to a game — new features, characters, or rules. Modding is many kids’ first taste of programming.
Insult for younger gamers whose voices haven’t dropped yet — the high-pitched kid in voice chat. Often your kid, sometimes affectionately.
“You’re playing like a computer NPC” — bad, predictable, brainless. The gaming insult that escaped into school hallways.
terms.example: “Missed an open shot? You a bot.”

terms.definition: Paid randomized rewards — real money for a chance at rare skins/items. Widely criticized as gambling-adjacent for kids; some countries regulate them.
terms.example: “He spent $40 on loot boxes and got nothing good.”

terms.definition: Per Axis: often sarcastic — a too-wide smile masking displeasure, like the single-tear emoji. Context: “Great, another group project 😃”.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Usually NOT sad — something was so funny (or shocking) it brought tears. The laughing emoji of Gen Z/Alpha, alongside 💀.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Soft sadness, vulnerability, or begging — often paired with 👉👈. “Can we get McDonald’s 🥺”.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Smiling through despair — things are hanging by a thread but we’re laughing about it. “Said ‘love you’ to my teacher 🥲”.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Overwhelmed, dread, dissolving under pressure — the burnout emoji.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Respectful agreement — “yes sir/ma’am,” mission accepted. Sincere or playfully formal.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Hiding after saying something bold or confessing — softens the message. “I forgot to defrost the chicken 🫣”.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Suspicion — “explain yourself.” The digital side-eye.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Per Axis: silliness that lightens something disappointing — “Got an F on my final 🤪”. Coping, not just goofing.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Smiling through the pain — yee-haw on the outside, crisis on the inside. Same coping family as 🤪.
terms.example: “hosting both sides of the family this year 🤠”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Giddy excitement or delighted gossip — the “oooooh” emoji.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Head in the clouds, zoned out, mentally elsewhere — or deliberately oblivious.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: At a loss for words — speechless, awkward silence.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Shock or judgment — the flushed wide-eyed stare.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Contained excitement, staged nonchalance — pretending to be chill about something great.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Per Axis: reads as outdated, sarcastic, or passive-aggressive to teens — “Thanks for ruining the surprise 👍”. Parents mean it sincerely; kids receive it cold. A genuine generational divider.
terms.example: A bare 👍 reply can end a group chat conversation.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Sassy affirmation, unbothered energy, “and that’s that.” Axis notes a negative use: insinuating a guy is being fruity.
terms.example: “Told him no and went back to my show 💅”
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Flirting — usually sarcastic/ironic per Axis (“love when he wears cargo shorts 🫦”), but genuinely suggestive in DMs. Context matters.
terms.example: Ironic thirst in comments; real thirst in DMs.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Someone is so attractive that just looking at them “got me pregnant.” Hyperbolic thirst compliment.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Per Axis: going in blind — knowingly making a bad decision while ignoring the red flags.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Desperate pleading — on knees, begging. “DROP THE ALBUM 🧎”.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Shyness or playful embarrassment.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Mood-lightener and ironic emphasis — “spilled coffee on my white pants ✨”. Also decorates genuinely aesthetic things. (See fairy sparkles 🧚✨ for the mean version.)
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Love/support — the young replacement for a plain ❤️.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Thank you, please, or gratitude. (Prayer or high-five depending on who you ask — teens mean thanks.)
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Dead-on accurate — “exactly right.”
terms.example: Reply to a hot take that nails it: 🎯
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Things going well (📈) or badly (📉) — applied to anything: grades, vibes, friendships, aura.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Comic frustration — “I’m upset about this” with a toy-gun punchline (the emoji replaced the realistic pistol years ago). Same job as 🔪: humor, not threat. Genuine threats read very differently in context.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Humorous outrage — dramatic “I could kill” energy about minor grievances. As with 🔫, context separates joke from genuine concern.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Love — and, per Axis, a softener for rejection (“I can’t come ❤️”). The heart-color hierarchy is its own teen politics.
terms.sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Emoji (2026)

terms.definition: Address — “send the addy.” (Older drug slang used it for Adderall; today’s teens mostly mean location. Context check.)
terms.example: “Mom can drop me — what’s the addy?”

terms.definition: A mom with restrictive diet-culture habits who pushes them on her kids (“just eat a few almonds”). Opposite: butter mom, who promotes moderate, normal eating.
A compliment on someone’s body/figure. From “tea” = the goods.
terms.example: “Did you see her prom dress? Body tea.”

terms.definition: “Get out of here” — dismissing someone who’s annoyed you, as if summoning their ride home.
terms.example: “You did NOT just say that. Call yo Uber.”

terms.definition: Caucasian + audacity — behavior displaying white privilege/obliviousness. Pointed humor.
terms.example: “Shoes on in the house? The caucasity.”

terms.definition: To say/do something deliberately provocative as a joke — “woke up and chose violence.”
terms.example: “He put the cast iron in the dishwasher. Chose violence.”

terms.definition: A loser. Started as a movie acronym (Cannibalistic Humanoid Underground Dweller), passed through politics, generalized to any basement-dweller insult.

terms.definition: Three uses per Axis: killed off (gaming), exposed/caught in a bad moment (social), or photographed unready.
Crude terms for a promiscuous guy (dih) or girl (puh) — “community property” implication. Slut-shaming language parents should recognize.
terms.example: Heard in gossip; worth a values conversation.

terms.definition: Deep immersion where everything clicks — borrowed from psychology, used for study sessions and games going perfectly.
terms.example: “Three hours of homework, full flow state.”

terms.definition: Out-shined in a photo — someone looked better than you in the same frame. From mogging.
terms.example: “My sister frame mogged me in the Christmas card.”

terms.definition: Friend/buddy — “that’s my G.” Old-school, still current.
Crunchy-outdoorsy aesthetic — Birkenstocks, hiking, organic food, small-business energy.
Used (clinically incorrectly) for impulsive urges — “let the intrusive thoughts win” = got 2am Taco Bell. The real psychiatric term means unwanted distressing thoughts; kids mean whims.
terms.example: “Intrusive thoughts won: I bleached my hair.”

terms.definition: Live-action role play — literally costumes in the park; figuratively, an insult for someone pretending to be what they aren’t.
Intensifier — “very”: mad expensive, mad late. NY classic still in rotation.
Suffix for maximizing anything: proteinmaxxing, sleepmaxxing, gymmaxxing. Escaped from looksmaxxing into general self-improvement talk.
Keeping plans private until they succeed — announce the win, not the attempt.
terms.example: “Started training months ago. Moving in silence.”

terms.definition: Overwhelmed — sensory or emotional. Therapy-speak that went mainstream with teens.
Money. “Getting paper” = earning.
A commoner/lower-class person — derogatory, from Roman “plebeian.” Gaming and school-status teasing.
Keeping something on the down-low — deliberately fuzzy meaning, from a Saucy Santana song about not scaring the fish.
terms.example: “New relationship? Quiet on the creek for now.”

terms.definition: Derogatory: sexually experienced with many partners. Slut-shaming term — flagged for parents in Axis’s explicit-content list.
Affirmation of authenticity — the one-word “I agree completely.”
Joke label for any small austerity — skipping Starbucks, shorter nails, rewearing outfits. Economic anxiety as meme.
A worse version of something that was better the first time — sequels, trends, copycats.
A lifestyle of ease and low stress as the goal — the anti-grind aspiration.
terms.example: “Finals done. Entering my soft life era.”

terms.definition: Making yourself the center of attention — like it’s your birthday — flattering or not.
terms.example: “Showed up in a suit to a picnic. You the birthday.”

terms.definition: A cartridge for a vape pen — usually THC oil. “Carts” in a teen’s texts are rarely about shopping.
A vape pen — for nicotine or weed, cartridge-based. Looks like a USB drive or actual pen; easy to miss in a pencil case.
Ketamine — the dissociative anesthetic, not the cereal. Club-drug slang parents should recognize.
terms.example: Cereal talk in a party context isn’t about breakfast.

terms.definition: Cocaine — the two most common word-codes (alongside the ❄️ emoji family).
terms.example: “Snow” outside of weather talk deserves attention.

terms.definition: Having sex — current crude teen euphemism per Bark’s sexting guide.
Algospeak for “LGBTQ” — sounds it out to dodge moderation filters. Not derogatory in itself; context decides.
Algospeak for nipples — cutesy spelling to evade content filters.
A vibrator, per Bark’s sexting-code list — food-emoji language taken one step further.
Code for sex worker / OnlyFans creator — because nobody asks follow-up questions about a boring job. Parents seeing “accountant” jokes on TikTok now know.
The opposite of an almond mom — promotes sensible, moderate, guilt-free eating.
terms.example: “We have whole milk. I have a butter mom.”

terms.definition: “Down low” — keep it secret. “Keep it on the DL.”
terms.example: “We’re dating, keep it on the DL.”

terms.definition: For You Page — TikTok’s algorithmic home feed. “Made it to the FYP” = the algorithm blessed your video.
terms.example: “This dance is all over my FYP.”

terms.definition: Fill-in-the-blank callout of the one detail that makes or breaks something: “it’s the early mornings for me.” Praise or roast.
“Please tell me you’re joking right now” — the modern SIKE!, deployed at bad news.

terms.term: it really do be like that
terms.definition: “It is what it is” — resigned, relatable acceptance of life’s nonsense. Grammar intentionally loose.
terms.example: “Lost my headphones AND my keys.” “It really do be like that sometimes.”

terms.definition: The “shut up and take my money” trend — banging a credit card on the table for something you’d buy instantly. Comment-section spam: 💥💥💳💥💥.
The letter P + star emoji = “porn star” — filter-dodging code from TikTok. Same family as 🌽 and ⬛🟧.
terms.example: In bios and comments where the word would be blocked.
